# Four strands, and what each depends on


The first chapter named four strands and a reply. Each strand begins from its
own text and needs one disputed reading of it to reach the conclusion that the
Messiah would be born of a virgin. This chapter takes them in turn, then the
reply, then what the strands show together.

### Isaiah 7:14

The first strand is the one Matthew draws:

> "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name
> Immanuel." (Isaiah 7:14)

It reads the verse as foretelling a virgin birth, and it needs the word for the
woman, עַלְמָה (*almah*), to mean a virgin (`almahMeansVirgin`). That is where
the whole quarrel over the word is joined. Matthew's quotation and his intent
that the birth fulfil the verse are grounds of the strand too, and so is the
Septuagint's rendering, παρθένος.

The ancient translations are encoded in full, including the half that tells
against this reading. The Aramaic paraphrase of the prophets, Targum Jonathan,
renders עוּלֵימְתָא, "young woman", and does not read 7:14 of the Messiah,
though it reads 9:5–6 and 11:1 so. The later Greek translators Aquila,
Symmachus and Theodotion, "the Three", render νεᾶνις, "young woman".
On the other side, the pre-Christian Septuagint renders παρθένος, "virgin" on
Rico and Gentry's reading of its Greek, though not on Wegner's (the chapter
[What the Septuagint's word meant](septuagint.md)), and the Syriac Peshitta renders ܒܬܘܠܬܐ,
"virgin", its only ܒܬܘܠܬܐ for עַלְמָה. So the Aramaic evidence is itself split:
the Targum against the Peshitta, whose translator may have been a Jewish
Christian who knew the Greek (van der Kooij), and whose 7:14 may follow the
Septuagint (Chen).

The text itself is not in doubt. The great Isaiah scroll from Qumran, 1QIsaᵃ,
copied before Christ, reads עַלְמָה as the Masoretic Text does. The verse has
other variants, but none at the word, so no variant rescues either side: the
dispute is over the word's sense. The usual Christian reply, that the Three
revised their Greek against Christian use, is one party's ground and not the
library's: Rico and Gentry's case from usage leans on it, and Davidson and
Meade read the revision the other way. Whether Theodotion's version is itself
pre-Christian, which would give the revision a reason with no polemic in it,
the library has not yet found a source to cite, and it is left out of the
reckoning.

### Genesis 3:15

The second strand goes back to the garden, where God says to the serpent:

> "And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and
> her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel."
> (Genesis 3:15, KJV)

The strand reads the verse as the first promise of a redeemer, the
*protoevangelium* ("first gospel"), and takes its wording, "her seed" (זֶרַע
הָאִשָּׁה), to mark a birth with no human father, because Hebrew ordinarily
reckons seed through the man. That last step is contestable, and it is rated
`disputed`. Luther and Henry take it. Some who grant the promise deny it, the
Lutheran commentators Leupold and Keil among them. Leupold allows that the
wording refers to the virgin birth "Not primarily, but at least incidentally",
and holds that "the expression used does not specifically prophesy the virgin
birth, but it coincides and agrees with it under divine providence". And Genesis
itself speaks of a woman's seed in ordinary births, of Hagar's (16:10) and of
Rebekah's (24:60). The chapters [Does Genesis 3:15 rule out a human father?](her-seed.md) and
[Is Genesis 3:15 a promise, fulfilled in Jesus?](the-promise.md) weigh the strand.

### Micah 5:2–3

The third strand reads the prophecy of the ruler from Bethlehem. Israel will be
given up "until the time when she who is in labour has given birth" (Micah
5:3), and the strand takes that as naming a mother and no father for the coming
ruler. The objection is immediate, and it is encoded as the rival: this is an
argument from silence, and an oracle about a woman in labour has no occasion to
mention a father.

### Isaiah 2–12

The fourth strand declines the fight over the word altogether. Seth Postell
reads Isaiah 7 inside Isaiah 2–12, a unit framed by visions of the last days at
2:1–4 and 11:1–12:6. On the principle that an oracle's meaning in a finished
book is set by its place in the book, and not by the events it first spoke to,
which he argues from the making of canonical Jeremiah, 7:14 looks ahead to a
future and miraculous birth. The strand turns on that principle
(`compositionGovernsMeaning`), and a reader who holds that an oracle's
historical setting fixes its sense rejects it outright.

## The reply: a virgin is an *almah*

The referential reply answers the dispute over the word without entering it.
*Almah* need not *mean* "virgin" for Mary to *be* an *almah*. Genesis shows the
two words can name one woman: Rebekah is an עַלְמָה at 24:43, and at 24:16 a
virgin (בְּתוּלָה) "whom no man had known". Mary was a betrothed young woman of
marriageable age who conceived as a virgin, so she answers Isaiah's description
on anyone's dictionary, and Matthew's claim never required the sense the
objection demands (`semantic_establishes`).

The reply has a price. It is purely defensive: it takes away the objection and
delivers nothing in its place, so the conclusion still has to come from one of
the four strands (`compatibility_does_not_establish_criterion`). What it buys is
that *losing* the dispute over the word no longer costs Matthew his fulfilment.

It also changes what the translations show. Grant every one of them, add the
referential premises, and the objection from the versions no longer reaches its
conclusion (`compatibility_defeats_lexical_objection`). Once virginity is
compatible with the word, four translators making four different choices about
how much of the woman to make explicit tell us nothing about the word's sense.

## What the strands show together

No single disputed reading carries the argument. Strip the reading of *almah*
and the other three strands still deliver the conclusion
(`almah_not_load_bearing`). Strip all four disputed readings and it fails
(`hinges_jointly_load_bearing`). Genesis's strand delivers it only on Luther's
reading of "her seed", which nothing here forces (the chapter
[Does Genesis 3:15 rule out a human father?](her-seed.md)). Within the Isaianic strand taken
by itself, the reading of the word still carries everything, as it did before
the other strands were encoded (`almah_is_load_bearing_alone`).

None of this shows that the strands are secure. Each rests on a reading someone
competent denies. It shows that an opponent has to answer all four, and that
winning the argument over *almah* does not by itself defeat the conclusion.

What the strands share is the conception itself and its attestation. Matthew's
and Luke's birth narratives agree on the virgin conception while differing in
nearly every other detail, and that agreement is encoded as a premise of
independent attestation (`independentAttestation`). Whether the two traditions
are independent is itself debated, so it is rated `plausible`, not
`wellSupported`.

Luke is a second witness to the conception, not to the prophecy. His account
runs parallel to Matthew's and independent of it, but it never quotes Isaiah
7:14. Luke 1:31 is close to the Septuagint's wording, and whether that is an
allusion is disputed. The library records it as one, attributed
(`lukeAllusionEdge`), and records the rival reading beside it, on which the
wording is the stock form of a birth announcement, the form Isaiah 7:14 itself
uses (`annunciationFormEdge`). Luke adds to the attestation of the conception;
he adds nothing to the rating of the predictive reading.

## The positions, written out


Besides the scriptural case, built from the four strands, these positions are
written out:

- **Rome's**, which adds papal teaching on Mary's virginity to the four strands;
- **the critical denial**, which grants the texts and denies every inference
  drawn from them;
- **the objection from the ancient versions**, the Targum's "young woman" and
  the Three's νεᾶνις, with the referential reply set against it;
- **Wegner's objection**, at full strength, and in variants that take one of
  its grounds away to ask what supplies it;
- and the positions in the disputes over the sign, the Septuagint's word and
  "her seed", which the later chapters weigh.

Beside them are variants of the scriptural case. Each asks whether the case
depends on one premise: with it taken out, either the conclusion still follows,
or the checking names a way of taking the texts on which it does not.

## What follows, and what does not


Each result takes one position and asks whether its conclusion follows from its
premises. Where it does, the result says so. Where it does not, the result names
a consistent way of taking the texts on which every premise holds and the
conclusion fails. That way of taking them is the rival position, written down,
and a reader can check it verse by verse.

Many results ask what the case depends on. A premise is taken out, everything
else is kept, and the result says whether the conclusion still follows. If it
does, the case never needed that premise. The result to read first is the one
that asks it of all four strands at once (`hinges_jointly_load_bearing`).

The results about the critical denial and the replies to it are here too, and
the chapter [Was Isaiah's sign only for Ahaz?](ahaz.md) weighs them. The results about
Wegner's objection are in the chapter [Was the woman already pregnant?](wegner.md).

<a id="parityDefeatsNearTermExclusion"></a>
**`parityDefeatsNearTermExclusion`**

**Postell's parity argument.** Isaiah 9:5–6 and 11:1–10 are read as
messianic without reservation, and they stand on the same near-term Assyrian
timeline as 7:14 — the Assyrian invasion of 8:7–8, the oppressor's rod of 10:5.
So a near-term geopolitical setting cannot be what rules out messianic
reference, because if it were it would rule out 9 and 11 as well.

This is a second, independent defeater of the same critical step that Berry's
objection attacks, and it is the stronger of the two: Berry says the near-term
fulfilment is unclear, while parity says the near-term setting was never the
right kind of reason.

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-47}{P_{47}}\\) Isaiah 9:5–6 and 11:1–10 are read as messianic without reservation — *well supported*: [Postell 2025](../../bibliography.md#postell-isaiah-messianic-2025), pp. 487–489; [Chilton 1987](../../bibliography.md#chilton-isaiah-targum-1987)
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-48}{P_{48}}\\) Isaiah 9 and 11 sit on the same near-term Assyrian timeline as 7:14 — *well supported*: [Postell 2025](../../bibliography.md#postell-isaiah-messianic-2025), pp. 487–489; Isa 8:7-8; Isa 9:8-11; Isa 10:5
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-82}{P_{82}}\\) *denied:* A sign given for Ahaz's generation is not also a prediction of a virgin birth

</div>

##### The referential strand

Sense against reference. The steps below never claim that עַלְמָה *means*
virgin; they claim that a virgin *is* an עַלְמָה, which is a different and far
cheaper claim, and then ask what the lexical objection is left with.

<a id="toDescriptionFit"></a>
**`toDescriptionFit`**

If virginity is compatible with the denotation of עַלְמָה, and Mary was both
an עַלְמָה and a virgin, then Mary answers Isaiah's description — without the
word having to carry the sense.

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-4}{P_{4}}\\) עַלְמָה denotes a young woman of marriageable age — *consensus*: [Rico and Gentry 2020](../../bibliography.md#rico-gentry-infant-king-2020); [Wegner 2011](../../bibliography.md#wegner-virgin-births-2011)
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-5}{P_{5}}\\) Being a virgin does not exclude a woman from the denotation of עַלְמָה — *consensus*: Gen 24:43; Gen 24:16; [Rico and Gentry 2020](../../bibliography.md#rico-gentry-infant-king-2020)
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-6}{P_{6}}\\) Mary at the conception was a betrothed young woman of marriageable age — *consensus*: Matt 1:18; Luke 1:27; [France 2007](../../bibliography.md#france-matthew-2007), ad loc. Matt 1:23
- (4) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-79}{P_{79}}\\) Mary conceived Jesus while a virgin — *disputed*: Matt 1:18-25; Luke 1:26-38; [Brown 1972](../../bibliography.md#brown-problem-virginal-conception-1972), pp. 30–33
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-7}{P_{7}}\\) Mary answers the description at Isaiah 7:14 whatever עַלְמָה denotes

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\((\href{claims.html#claim-4}{P_{4}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-5}{P_{5}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-6}{P_{6}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-79}{P_{79}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-7}{P_{7}}\\).

- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-11}{P_{11}}\\) Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion render Isaiah 7:14 with νεᾶνις — *consensus*: [Rico and Gentry 2020](../../bibliography.md#rico-gentry-infant-king-2020); [Irenaeus](../../bibliography.md#irenaeus-against-heresies-180), §III.21.1; [Eusebius of Caesarea](../../bibliography.md#eusebius-demonstratio-evangelica-315), §VII.1

<a id="compatibilityDissolvesDivergence"></a>
**`compatibilityDissolvesDivergence`**

**The tension, dissolved.** If virginity is compatible with עַלְמָה, the
versions are not contradicting one another about the referent at all: the
Septuagint, if its παρθένος already meant "virgin" (`Dispute.Septuagint`), and
the Peshitta render with the narrower term, the Targum and the Three with the
broader one, and both are faithful renderings of a word whose denotation admits
both. The divergence stops being evidence about the sense.

Why the Peshitta has the narrower term is not settled. It is its only ܒܬܘܠܬܐ for
עַלְמָה, and whether that is its translator's reading of the woman, the
Septuagint's influence, or a later Christian hand, Chen finds impossible to
decide (104–5). The step needs only that the rendering is a faithful one, not
why it was chosen.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) The Septuagint renders עַלְמָה at Isaiah 7:14 as παρθένος — *consensus*: [Aland et al. 2012](../../bibliography.md#na28-2012), app. Matt 1:23; [France 2007](../../bibliography.md#france-matthew-2007), ad loc. Matt 1:23
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-12}{P_{12}}\\) The Syriac Peshitta renders Isaiah 7:14 with ܒܬܘܠܬܐ, 'virgin' — *consensus*: Isa 7:14; [van der Kooij 1981](../../bibliography.md#van-der-kooij-textzeugen-jesajabuches-1981), p. 271; Gen 24:43; Exod 2:8; Ps 68:26; Song 1:3; Song 6:8; [Bloch 1919](../../bibliography.md#bloch-authorship-peshitta-1919), pp. 218–219; [Chen 2020](../../bibliography.md#chen-peshitta-isaiah-2020), pp. 104–105
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-14}{P_{14}}\\) *denied:* The split among the ancient versions shows עַלְמָה does not denote virginity

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\((\href{claims.html#claim-5}{P_{5}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-12}{P_{12}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-14}{P_{14}}\\).

##### Wegner's grammatical objection, and the circle Postell finds in it

The sharpest form of the lexical case. Each link is a step of its own, because
the result worth having is not whether the objection is valid — it is — but
which link carries its weight, and where that link comes from.

<a id="harahYieldsPresentPregnancy"></a>
**`harahYieldsPresentPregnancy`**

Wegner's grammatical step: if הָרָה is a predicate adjective, the עַלְמָה of
the sign is pregnant already, at the moment the sign is given.

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-33}{P_{33}}\\) הָרָה at Isaiah 7:14 is a predicate adjective: the עַלְמָה is pregnant — *well supported*: [Wegner 2011](../../bibliography.md#wegner-virgin-births-2011), p. 471; [Postell 2025](../../bibliography.md#postell-isaiah-messianic-2025), p. 474; [Young 1953](../../bibliography.md#young-immanuel-prophecy-1953), pp. 115–116
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-34}{P_{34}}\\) The עַלְמָה of Isaiah 7:14 is already pregnant when the sign is given

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\(\href{claims.html#claim-33}{P_{33}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-34}{P_{34}}\\).

<a id="ordinaryPregnancyExcludesVirginity"></a>
**`ordinaryPregnancyExcludesVirginity`**

... and if that pregnancy is an ordinary conception, the woman it describes
is not a virgin.

The second conjunct does all the work, and it is not a grammatical claim.
Rydelnik parses הָרָה exactly as Wegner does and reads the same clause as the
miracle itself — the virgin *is* pregnant — which is available to him precisely
because the parse leaves this open.

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-34}{P_{34}}\\) The עַלְמָה of Isaiah 7:14 is already pregnant when the sign is given — *well supported*: [Wegner 2011](../../bibliography.md#wegner-virgin-births-2011), pp. 471–472; [Postell 2025](../../bibliography.md#postell-isaiah-messianic-2025), p. 468; [Young 1953](../../bibliography.md#young-immanuel-prophecy-1953), pp. 116–117
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}\\) The pregnancy Isaiah 7:14 announces is an ordinary conception — *disputed*: [Wegner 2011](../../bibliography.md#wegner-virgin-births-2011), pp. 476–478; [Postell 2025](../../bibliography.md#postell-isaiah-messianic-2025), p. 474
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-36}{P_{36}}\\) The עַלְמָה of Isaiah 7:14 is not a virgin

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\((\href{claims.html#claim-34}{P_{34}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-36}{P_{36}}\\).

<a id="referentYieldsLexicalConclusion"></a>
**`referentYieldsLexicalConclusion`**

... and if what the one clear Isaianic referent turns out to be settles what
the word denotes, the lexical conclusion follows.

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-36}{P_{36}}\\) The עַלְמָה of Isaiah 7:14 is not a virgin — *disputed*: [Wegner 2011](../../bibliography.md#wegner-virgin-births-2011), pp. 471–472; [Postell 2025](../../bibliography.md#postell-isaiah-messianic-2025), p. 468
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\) What the עַלְמָה of Isaiah 7:14 turns out to be settles what the word denotes — *disputed*: [Wegner 2011](../../bibliography.md#wegner-virgin-births-2011), pp. 471–472; [Postell 2025](../../bibliography.md#postell-isaiah-messianic-2025), p. 468; [Rico and Gentry 2020](../../bibliography.md#rico-gentry-infant-king-2020), p. 152
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\) *denied:* עַלְמָה in Isaiah 7:14 denotes a virgin, not merely a young woman

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\((\href{claims.html#claim-36}{P_{36}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-37}{P_{37}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\).

<a id="readingSuppliesOrdinaryPregnancy"></a>
**`readingSuppliesOrdinaryPregnancy`**

**Where the ordinary pregnancy comes from.** Not from the grammar: from the
near-term reading of the sign, which has the child born within nine months and
the whole oracle discharged by 701 BC.

This is Postell's charge, written as a formula rather than repeated as a
complaint: "because Wegner rejects the messianic interpretation on
grammatical-historical grounds, he assumes that עַלְמָה cannot mean 'virgin' in
Isaiah 7:14" (468 n. 22).

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-81}{P_{81}}\\) Isaiah 7:14 is a near-term sign to Ahaz, fulfilled in Isaiah's generation — *disputed*: [Brown 1993](../../bibliography.md#brown-birth-messiah-1993)
- (2) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-1}{P_{1}}\\) *denied:* Isaiah 7:14 is a Messianic prediction of a virgin birth — *disputed*: [Motyer 1993](../../bibliography.md#motyer-isaiah-1993), ad loc. Isa 7:14; [Motyer 1970](../../bibliography.md#motyer-context-content-1970), p. 123; [Compton 2007](../../bibliography.md#compton-immanuel-prophecy-2007), pp. 12–14; [Justin Martyr](../../bibliography.md#justin-dialogue-with-trypho-160), §66; [Irenaeus](../../bibliography.md#irenaeus-against-heresies-180), §III.21.6; [Origen](../../bibliography.md#origen-against-celsus-248), §I.35
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}\\) The pregnancy Isaiah 7:14 announces is an ordinary conception

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\((\href{claims.html#claim-81}{P_{81}} \land \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-1}{P_{1}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}\\).

<a id="lexicalConclusionTellsAgainstPrediction"></a>
**`lexicalConclusionTellsAgainstPrediction`**

**The return leg.** The lexical conclusion is then turned against the
predictive reading, which is what the critical case does with it and what
`critical` already assumes.

Wegner's own version of this step is weaker — Postell reports it as decreasing
the likelihood of a virgin-birth prediction without ruling it out (469) — and
the encoding states the strong form on purpose. The strong form is the one on
which the two legs make a closed circle, and stating it is what lets
`circle_leaves_the_lexical_conclusion_open` be checked rather than asserted. On
the weaker
form the loop is evidential rather than deductive, which is the difference
between a vicious circle and mutual support.

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\) *denied:* עַלְמָה in Isaiah 7:14 denotes a virgin, not merely a young woman — *disputed*: [Motyer 1993](../../bibliography.md#motyer-isaiah-1993), ad loc. Isa 7:14; [Elliger and Rudolph 1997](../../bibliography.md#bhs-1997), app. Isa 7:14; [Berry 2003](../../bibliography.md#berry-virgin-birth-2003), pp. 1653–1654; [Motyer 1970](../../bibliography.md#motyer-context-content-1970), p. 125; [Compton 2007](../../bibliography.md#compton-immanuel-prophecy-2007), pp. 7–8; [Jerome](../../bibliography.md#jerome-against-jovinianus-393), §I.32
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-8}{P_{8}}\\) Matthew's fulfilment claim requires that עַלְמָה itself denote virginity — *disputed*: [Brown 1993](../../bibliography.md#brown-birth-messiah-1993)
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-1}{P_{1}}\\) *denied:* Isaiah 7:14 is a Messianic prediction of a virgin birth

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\((\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-8}{P_{8}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-1}{P_{1}}\\).

<a id="usageParityBlocksReferentInference"></a>
**`usageParityBlocksReferentInference`**

**Postell's usage parity.** If a single clear referent settled the
denotation, the other clear עַלְמָה passages would settle it in the opposite
direction, since the women there are virgins. So that principle is not
available to the objection: it proves too much, and the wrong way.

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-38}{P_{38}}\\) In the other clear עַלְמָה passages Wegner lists, the women are virgins — *plausible*: [Postell 2025](../../bibliography.md#postell-isaiah-messianic-2025), p. 468; [Wegner 2011](../../bibliography.md#wegner-virgin-births-2011), pp. 471–472; [Jerome](../../bibliography.md#jerome-against-jovinianus-393), §I.32; [Compton 2007](../../bibliography.md#compton-immanuel-prophecy-2007), p. 8; Gen 24:43; Song 6:8
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\) *denied:* What the עַלְמָה of Isaiah 7:14 turns out to be settles what the word denotes

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\(\href{claims.html#claim-38}{P_{38}} \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\).

##### The fathers' sign argument, and the near-term reply

Wegner's objection needs the pregnancy to be an ordinary one. The oldest
Christian answer to the near-term reading denies exactly that, and it does so
without touching the word: the oracle promised a *sign*, and an ordinary
conception would have been none.

<a id="extraordinarySignExcludesOrdinaryPregnancy"></a>
**`extraordinarySignExcludesOrdinaryPregnancy`**

**The sign argument.** If the sign of 7:14 must be extraordinary, and an
ordinary conception is nothing extraordinary, the pregnancy the sign announces
is not an ordinary one.

The step assumes that the conception is the sign rather than one part of it.
Wegner counts three parts in 7:14 and more in 7:15–16 (469, 477), but he does
not grant the first ground and deny the conclusion: he denies the first
ground.

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-39}{P_{39}}\\) The sign of Isaiah 7:14 must be extraordinary, like the sign offered at 7:11 — *disputed*: [Origen](../../bibliography.md#origen-against-celsus-248), §I.35; [Justin Martyr](../../bibliography.md#justin-dialogue-with-trypho-160), §84; [Irenaeus](../../bibliography.md#irenaeus-against-heresies-180), §III.21.6; [Tertullian](../../bibliography.md#tertullian-answer-to-the-jews-200), §9; [Eusebius of Caesarea](../../bibliography.md#eusebius-demonstratio-evangelica-315), §VII.1; [Cyril of Jerusalem](../../bibliography.md#cyril-jerusalem-catechetical-lectures-350), §12.22; [John Chrysostom](../../bibliography.md#chrysostom-homilies-matthew-390), §5; [Jerome](../../bibliography.md#jerome-commentary-isaiah-410), ad loc. Isa 7:14; [Cyril of Alexandria](../../bibliography.md#cyril-alexandria-commentary-isaiah), ad loc. Isa 7:14; [Theodoret of Cyrrhus](../../bibliography.md#theodoret-commentary-isaiah), ad loc. Isa 7:14; [Postell 2025](../../bibliography.md#postell-isaiah-messianic-2025), p. 474; Isa 7:10-11
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-40}{P_{40}}\\) An ordinary conception is nothing extraordinary: it happens to all women — *consensus*: [Irenaeus](../../bibliography.md#irenaeus-against-heresies-180), §III.21.6; [Justin Martyr](../../bibliography.md#justin-dialogue-with-trypho-160), §84; [Rhodea 2013](../../bibliography.md#rhodea-did-matthew-conceive-2013), p. 64
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}\\) *denied:* The pregnancy Isaiah 7:14 announces is an ordinary conception

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\((\href{claims.html#claim-39}{P_{39}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-40}{P_{40}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}\\).

<a id="ordinarySignsAnswerTheDemand"></a>
**`ordinarySignsAnswerTheDemand`**

**The near-term reply.** Signs elsewhere in Isaiah are ordinary events, and
this one is dated by a child's infancy, so its point is its timing and it need
not be extraordinary.

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}}\\) Signs elsewhere in Isaiah are ordinary events: his children, 8:18 — *consensus*: Isa 8:18; Isa 20:3; Isa 37:30; [Rhodea 2013](../../bibliography.md#rhodea-did-matthew-conceive-2013), p. 64; [Wegner 2011](../../bibliography.md#wegner-virgin-births-2011), p. 470
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}\\) Isaiah 7:16 dates the deliverance by a child's infancy — *consensus*: Isa 7:16; [Wegner 2011](../../bibliography.md#wegner-virgin-births-2011), p. 477; [Compton 2007](../../bibliography.md#compton-immanuel-prophecy-2007), p. 14
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-39}{P_{39}}\\) *denied:* The sign of Isaiah 7:14 must be extraordinary, like the sign offered at 7:11

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\((\href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-39}{P_{39}}\\).

##### The Septuagint, and what its word meant

Jews translated Isaiah into Greek before Christ and wrote παρθένος. What that
shows depends on what παρθένος meant to them, and the steps below keep the two
questions apart: what the translator wrote, and what the word he wrote meant.

<a id="septuagintReadsAVirgin"></a>
**`septuagintReadsAVirgin`**

**The Septuagint as a witness.** A Jewish translator, before Christ, chose
for the woman of 7:14 a word that means a virgin; so he read her as one.

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) The Septuagint renders עַלְמָה at Isaiah 7:14 as παρθένος — *consensus*: [Aland et al. 2012](../../bibliography.md#na28-2012), app. Matt 1:23; [France 2007](../../bibliography.md#france-matthew-2007), ad loc. Matt 1:23
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-15}{P_{15}}\\) The Greek Isaiah was translated by Jews before the coming of Christ — *consensus*: [Irenaeus](../../bibliography.md#irenaeus-against-heresies-180), §III.21.1; [Justin Martyr](../../bibliography.md#justin-dialogue-with-trypho-160), §71; [John Chrysostom](../../bibliography.md#chrysostom-homilies-matthew-390), §5; [Eusebius of Caesarea](../../bibliography.md#eusebius-demonstratio-evangelica-315), §VII.1; [Wegner 2011](../../bibliography.md#wegner-virgin-births-2011), p. 483
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-16}{P_{16}}\\) In the Greek of the Septuagint, παρθένος means a virgin — *disputed*: [Rico and Gentry 2020](../../bibliography.md#rico-gentry-infant-king-2020), p. 21; [Bratcher 1958](../../bibliography.md#bratcher-study-of-isaiah-1958), p. 113; [Postell 2025](../../bibliography.md#postell-isaiah-messianic-2025), p. 472
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-31}{P_{31}}\\) Before Christ, a Jewish translator read the woman of Isaiah 7:14 as a virgin

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\((\href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-15}{P_{15}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-16}{P_{16}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-31}{P_{31}}\\).

<a id="dinahShowsTheOlderSense"></a>
**`dinahShowsTheOlderSense`**

**Wegner's case that the word's sense shifted.** In early Greek παρθένος
meant a young woman, with or without virginity; the Septuagint calls Dinah one
at 34:3, and the noun there describes her as she then was, no longer a virgin;
so in the Septuagint's day the word meant "young woman", and the sense "virgin"
came later.

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-18}{P_{18}}\\) In early Greek, παρθένος meant a young woman, with or without virginity — *well supported*: [Wegner 2011](../../bibliography.md#wegner-virgin-births-2011), p. 482; [Rhodea 2013](../../bibliography.md#rhodea-did-matthew-conceive-2013), p. 67; [Bauer 2000](../../bibliography.md#bauer-danker-lexicon-2000), p. 777; [Liddell and Scott 1940](../../bibliography.md#liddell-scott-jones-lexicon-1940), p. 1339; [Walton 1987](../../bibliography.md#walton-whats-in-a-name-1987), p. 293; [Bratcher 1958](../../bibliography.md#bratcher-study-of-isaiah-1958), p. 112
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-19}{P_{19}}\\) The Septuagint calls Dinah a παρθένος at 34:3, after Shechem lies with her (34:2) — *consensus*: Gen 34:2-3; Gen 34:3; [Wegner 2011](../../bibliography.md#wegner-virgin-births-2011), p. 483; [Rhodea 2013](../../bibliography.md#rhodea-did-matthew-conceive-2013), p. 67; [Rico and Gentry 2020](../../bibliography.md#rico-gentry-infant-king-2020), pp. 18–21; [Bratcher 1958](../../bibliography.md#bratcher-study-of-isaiah-1958), p. 113
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-76}{P_{76}}\\) At 34:3 παρθένος describes Dinah as she then was, no longer a virgin (Miller) — *well supported*: [Miller 2003](../../bibliography.md#miller-born-divine-2003); [Wegner 2011](../../bibliography.md#wegner-virgin-births-2011), p. 483; [Muraoka 2009](../../bibliography.md#muraoka-lexicon-septuagint-2009), p. 535
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-17}{P_{17}}\\) In the Septuagint's day, παρθένος meant 'young woman'; not yet 'virgin'

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\((\href{claims.html#claim-18}{P_{18}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-19}{P_{19}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-76}{P_{76}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-17}{P_{17}}\\).

<a id="usageShowsTheVirginSense"></a>
**`usageShowsTheVirginSense`**

**The case from usage.** Rico and Gentry's: the Jews who rejected the
Christian reading of 7:14 rejected the word itself, Trypho reading "the young
woman" and the Three writing νεᾶνις. With it the library's own addition: the
Greek Isaiah's παρθένος renders בְּתוּלָה wherever else it occurs. So the word
meant a virgin.

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-20}{P_{20}}\\) Elsewhere in the Greek Isaiah, παρθένος renders בְּתוּלָה — *consensus*: Isa 23:4; Isa 23:4; Isa 37:22; Isa 37:22; Isa 47:1; Isa 47:1; Isa 62:5; Isa 62:5
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-11}{P_{11}}\\) Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion render Isaiah 7:14 with νεᾶνις — *consensus*: [Rico and Gentry 2020](../../bibliography.md#rico-gentry-infant-king-2020); [Irenaeus](../../bibliography.md#irenaeus-against-heresies-180), §III.21.1; [Eusebius of Caesarea](../../bibliography.md#eusebius-demonstratio-evangelica-315), §VII.1
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-30}{P_{30}}\\) Trypho rejects the Septuagint's 'the virgin' and reads 'the young woman' — *consensus*: [Justin Martyr](../../bibliography.md#justin-dialogue-with-trypho-160), §67; [Justin Martyr](../../bibliography.md#justin-dialogue-with-trypho-160), §71
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-16}{P_{16}}\\) In the Greek of the Septuagint, παρθένος means a virgin

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\((\href{claims.html#claim-20}{P_{20}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-11}{P_{11}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-30}{P_{30}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-16}{P_{16}}\\).

<a id="translatorsReadingFixesTheWord"></a>
**`translatorsReadingFixesTheWord`**

**From the translator's reading to Isaiah's word.** If the first translator
read the woman of 7:14 as a virgin, the word Isaiah used of her denotes one.

The step the Septuagint is usually asked to take, and the one its grounds do not
supply: it has to be granted separately, and it is rated `disputed`.

Irenaeus takes it because he holds the Greek inspired: the seventy elders,
translating apart, agreed "in the very same words", so that "the Scriptures had
been interpreted by the inspiration of God" (*Against Heresies* III.21.2).

Bratcher and Brown grant the ground and deny the step. Bratcher holds that the
translator meant "a young woman, at that time virgin" (115), and that עַלְמָה "is
neutral, so far as virginity is concerned" (105): "even if in all occurrences of
the word in the Old Testament it were proven that the 'almah in each case was,
in fact, a virgin, that would not prove that 'almah in Isaiah 7:14 means
'virgin'" (106). Brown holds that the translator's choice "represented a
deliberate preference for understanding the young woman of Isa 7:14 as a
virgin" (*Birth of the Messiah* 148), and that עַלְמָה puts "no stress on her
virginity" (147). Walton, who doubts the ground itself, denies the step even if it
is granted: "it is illegitimate to use the LXX translation to override clear
lexical material in the Hebrew text", and "at best the LXX would indicate an
interpretational preference rather than a linguistic necessity" (293).

Bratcher's and Brown's reason is that a rendering can follow the woman described
rather than the word. The translator of Genesis wrote παρθένος for the עַלְמָה
Rebekah (24:43), whom the story has already called a virgin (24:16):
"historically correct — since Rebekah was a virgin", Bratcher says, but it "does
not precisely translate the Hebrew" (113). Jerome reads Rebekah the other way, as
showing that עַלְמָה denotes a virgin (*Against Jovinianus* I.32). Elsewhere the
Septuagint's translators render עַלְמָה with νεᾶνις four times (Exodus 2:8;
Psalm 67:26, 68:25 in English Bibles; Song 1:3; 6:8) and with νεότης, "youth",
once (Proverbs 30:19), as Rahlfs's text shows; Rhodea counts the νεᾶνις cases
(67 n. 34). These are other translators than Isaiah's, as the translator of
Genesis 34:3 is. That is also how this argument's referential strand reads the
versions
(`compatibilityDissolvesDivergence`).

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-31}{P_{31}}\\) Before Christ, a Jewish translator read the woman of Isaiah 7:14 as a virgin — *disputed*: [Irenaeus](../../bibliography.md#irenaeus-against-heresies-180), §III.21.1; [Bratcher 1958](../../bibliography.md#bratcher-study-of-isaiah-1958), pp. 115–116; [Rhodea 2013](../../bibliography.md#rhodea-did-matthew-conceive-2013), p. 67
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\) עַלְמָה in Isaiah 7:14 denotes a virgin, not merely a young woman

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\(\href{claims.html#claim-31}{P_{31}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\).

##### Genesis 3:15, and what "her seed" says of a father

The protoevangelium strand holds that the seed being named as the woman's marks
a birth with no human father. The steps below take apart what "marks" can mean:
that the wording itself signifies such a birth, which Luther argues and
Leupold, Keil and Lewis deny, or that it fits one once fulfilled, which Leupold
and Keil grant.

<a id="herSeedSignifiesNoFather"></a>
**`herSeedSignifiesNoFather`**

**Luther's step.** Genesis 3:15 names the seed as the woman's, it is the
first promise of a redeemer, and a man's seed is ordinarily reckoned through
him; so the wording itself signifies a birth with no human father.

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}}\\) Genesis 3:15 says that 'her seed' will strike the serpent's head — *consensus*: Gen 3:15; [Elliger and Rudolph 1997](../../bibliography.md#bhs-1997), app. Gen 3:15
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}}\\) Genesis 3:15 is the protoevangelium, the first promise of a redeemer — *disputed*: [Leupold 1942](../../bibliography.md#leupold-exposition-genesis-1942), p. 167; [Keil and Delitzsch 1866](../../bibliography.md#keil-delitzsch-pentateuch-1866), p. 102; [Miravalle 2014](../../bibliography.md#miravalle-meet-your-mother-2014); [Lewis 1991](../../bibliography.md#lewis-womans-seed-1991), p. 318
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-52}{P_{52}}\\) Hebrew זֶרַע is ordinarily reckoned through the father — *well supported*: [Lewis 1991](../../bibliography.md#lewis-womans-seed-1991), p. 299; [Calvin 1960](../../bibliography.md#calvin-institutes-1960), §II.13.3; [Elliger and Rudolph 1997](../../bibliography.md#bhs-1997), app. Gen 3:15
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-54}{P_{54}}\\) The wording 'her seed' itself signifies a birth with no human father

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\((\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-52}{P_{52}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-54}{P_{54}}\\).

<a id="posterityExplainsTheWording"></a>
**`posterityExplainsTheWording`**

**Leupold's step.** "Her seed" is first collective, the woman's posterity,
and the seed is named hers because the serpent deceived her; so the wording does
not itself signify a birth with no human father.

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}}\\) Genesis 3:15 says that 'her seed' will strike the serpent's head — *consensus*: Gen 3:15; [Elliger and Rudolph 1997](../../bibliography.md#bhs-1997), app. Gen 3:15
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-56}{P_{56}}\\) 'Her seed' at Genesis 3:15 is first collective: her posterity, not one person — *disputed*: [Leupold 1942](../../bibliography.md#leupold-exposition-genesis-1942), pp. 167–169; [Calvin 1847](../../bibliography.md#calvin-commentary-genesis-1847), p. 170; [Keil and Delitzsch 1866](../../bibliography.md#keil-delitzsch-pentateuch-1866), p. 101; [Collins 1997](../../bibliography.md#collins-syntactical-note-1997), pp. 145–146
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-57}{P_{57}}\\) The seed is called the woman's because the serpent deceived the woman — *well supported*: [Leupold 1942](../../bibliography.md#leupold-exposition-genesis-1942), p. 165; [Leupold 1942](../../bibliography.md#leupold-exposition-genesis-1942), p. 169; [Calvin 1847](../../bibliography.md#calvin-commentary-genesis-1847), p. 170; [Henry 1706](../../bibliography.md#henry-commentary-whole-bible), ad loc. Gen 3:15; [Keil and Delitzsch 1866](../../bibliography.md#keil-delitzsch-pentateuch-1866), p. 102
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-54}{P_{54}}\\) *denied:* The wording 'her seed' itself signifies a birth with no human father

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\((\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-56}{P_{56}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-57}{P_{57}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-54}{P_{54}}\\).

<a id="ordinaryBirthsAnswerTheWording"></a>
**`ordinaryBirthsAnswerTheWording`**

**Lewis's step.** Genesis speaks of a woman's seed in ordinary births too;
so the woman's seed at 3:15 does not by itself signify a birth with no human
father.

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}}\\) Genesis 3:15 says that 'her seed' will strike the serpent's head — *consensus*: Gen 3:15; [Elliger and Rudolph 1997](../../bibliography.md#bhs-1997), app. Gen 3:15
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-58}{P_{58}}\\) Genesis speaks of a woman's seed in ordinary births: Hagar's and Rebekah's — *consensus*: Gen 16:10; Gen 24:60; [Lewis 1991](../../bibliography.md#lewis-womans-seed-1991), pp. 299–300
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-54}{P_{54}}\\) *denied:* The wording 'her seed' itself signifies a birth with no human father

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\((\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-58}{P_{58}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-54}{P_{54}}\\).

<a id="heReadsOneDescendant"></a>
**`heReadsOneDescendant`**

**The Greek's "he".** The Greek refers to the neuter seed with a masculine
pronoun; so its translator read the seed as one person.

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-59}{P_{59}}\\) The Greek of Genesis 3:15 calls the woman's seed 'he', though σπέρμα is neuter — *consensus*: Gen 3:15; [Collins 1997](../../bibliography.md#collins-syntactical-note-1997), p. 141
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-60}{P_{60}}\\) The Greek translator of Genesis read the woman's seed at 3:15 as one person

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\(\href{claims.html#claim-59}{P_{59}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-60}{P_{60}}\\).

##### The lines of reason

Four strands converge on the criterion, and each is a `Line`: its own grounds,
its own licensing step, and what it delivers. The packages are assembled from
these rather than from flat premise lists, so a variant package is a *named
difference* — one line on different grounds — instead of twenty premises retyped
with one missing.

`grounds` are the premises a line contributes of its own. What the strands hold
in common (Mary's conception, the agreement of the two narratives) is passed to
`caseOf` as shared, because it belongs to no single strand.

<a id="isaianicLine"></a>
**`isaianicLine`** — Isaianic strand (Isaiah 7:14)

**The Isaianic line.** The predictive reading, the lexical premise, the
Septuagint's rendering, and Matthew's quotation and intent. Its hinge is
`almahMeansVirgin`, and the whole lexical dispute is about that one ground.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-1}{P_{1}}\\) — Isaiah 7:14 is a Messianic prediction of a virgin birth
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\) — עַלְמָה in Isaiah 7:14 denotes a virgin, not merely a young woman
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — The Septuagint renders עַלְמָה at Isaiah 7:14 as παρθένος
- (4) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\) — Matthew 1:23 quotes Isaiah 7:14
- (5) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-44}{P_{44}}\\) — Matthew's quotation intends the virgin conception as fulfilment
- (6) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-1}{P_{1}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-44}{P_{44}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-93}{P_{93}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-93}{P_{93}}\\) — *at issue:* The Messiah must be born of a virgin

</div>

<a id="protoevangeliumLine"></a>
**`protoevangeliumLine`** — Protoevangelium strand (Genesis 3:15)

**The protoevangelium line.** Genesis 3:15 read as the promise of a
redeemer, a man's line counted through the father, and the claim that naming the
seed as the woman's marks a birth with no human father. That claim is its hinge
(`seedOfTheWomanImpliesNoHumanFather`), and `Results.Genesis` says what it can
bear, read either way.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}}\\) — Genesis 3:15 says that 'her seed' will strike the serpent's head
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}}\\) — Genesis 3:15 is the protoevangelium, the first promise of a redeemer
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-52}{P_{52}}\\) — Hebrew זֶרַע is ordinarily reckoned through the father
- (4) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-53}{P_{53}}\\) — The matrilineal wording of Genesis 3:15 marks a birth with no human father
- (5) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-52}{P_{52}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-53}{P_{53}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-93}{P_{93}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-93}{P_{93}}\\) — *at issue:* The Messiah must be born of a virgin

</div>

<a id="micheanLine"></a>
**`micheanLine`** — Michean strand (Micah 5:2–3)

**The Michean line.** The maternal-only wording of Micah 5:3 and the
inference drawn from it. Its hinge is an argument from silence, and the rival
says so.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-77}{P_{77}}\\) — Micah 5:3 names only the woman in labour as bearing the coming ruler
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-78}{P_{78}}\\) — Micah's mention of a mother and no father indicates a birth with no human father
- (3) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-77}{P_{77}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-78}{P_{78}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-93}{P_{93}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-93}{P_{93}}\\) — *at issue:* The Messiah must be born of a virgin

</div>

<a id="compositionalLine"></a>
**`compositionalLine`** — Compositional strand (Isaiah 2–12)

**The compositional line.** Isaiah 7's placement in an eschatologically
framed unit, the principle that placement governs meaning, and the future birth
that follows. Its hinge is `compositionGovernsMeaning`.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-45}{P_{45}}\\) — Isaiah 7 sits inside Isaiah 2–12, a unit framed by eschatology
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-46}{P_{46}}\\) — An oracle's meaning in the finished book is set by its literary placement
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-49}{P_{49}}\\) — Read compositionally, Isaiah 7:14 anticipates a future, miraculous birth
- (4) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-45}{P_{45}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-46}{P_{46}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-49}{P_{49}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-44}{P_{44}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-93}{P_{93}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-93}{P_{93}}\\) — *at issue:* The Messiah must be born of a virgin

</div>

<a id="magisterialLine"></a>
**`magisterialLine`** — Magisterial strand (papal teaching)

**The magisterial line.** Papal teaching and the authority granted it.

Encoded as a line like the others and deliberately kept out of `christian`: its
second ground is one this library's author does not grant. Keeping it a line
rather than folding it into a package is what lets
`magisterial_authority_is_load_bearing` ask what the route is worth on its
own.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-90}{P_{90}}\\) — Papal teaching affirms that Mary conceived while remaining a virgin
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-91}{P_{91}}\\) — Magisterial teaching settles the question
- (3) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-90}{P_{90}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-91}{P_{91}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-93}{P_{93}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-93}{P_{93}}\\) — *at issue:* The Messiah must be born of a virgin

</div>

<a id="referentialLine"></a>
**`referentialLine`** — Referential reading: a virgin is an עַלְמָה

**The referential line.** The shared lexical ground, the Rebekah datum,
and two claims about Mary — that she was a young woman of marriageable age, and
that she conceived as a virgin, which is cited `disputed` — delivering that she
answers Isaiah's description without the word having to carry the sense. The
fathers answer the Jewish "young woman" the same way: Cyril of Alexandria, "even
if the virgin were called a young woman, she will not cease to be a virgin".

The scroll's reading is a ground because the reply is about what the word
means, not which word Isaiah wrote: 1QIsaᵃ, copied before Christ, has the
Masoretic Text's עַלְמָה. If the Hebrew were in doubt the dispute would not be
about the sense alone, and the reply would have more to answer.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-4}{P_{4}}\\) — עַלְמָה denotes a young woman of marriageable age
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-5}{P_{5}}\\) — Being a virgin does not exclude a woman from the denotation of עַלְמָה
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-6}{P_{6}}\\) — Mary at the conception was a betrothed young woman of marriageable age
- (4) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-79}{P_{79}}\\) — Mary conceived Jesus while a virgin
- (5) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\) — 1QIsaᵃ, copied before Christ, reads הָעַלְמָה at Isaiah 7:14, as the Masoretic Text
- (6) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-4}{P_{4}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-5}{P_{5}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-6}{P_{6}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-79}{P_{79}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-7}{P_{7}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-7}{P_{7}}\\) — *at issue:* Mary answers the description at Isaiah 7:14 whatever עַלְמָה denotes

</div>

<a id="versionalLine"></a>
**`versionalLine`** — Lexical objection from the ancient versions

**The versional line**, stated as the objector would state it: the Targum
and the Three read the broad term, Qumran settles the Hebrew, and Matthew's
claim is taken to need the narrow sense — so the word does not denote
virginity.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-10}{P_{10}}\\) — Targum Jonathan renders עַלְמָה at Isaiah 7:14 as עוּלֵימְתָא, 'young woman'
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-11}{P_{11}}\\) — Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion render Isaiah 7:14 with νεᾶνις
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\) — 1QIsaᵃ, copied before Christ, reads הָעַלְמָה at Isaiah 7:14, as the Masoretic Text
- (4) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-14}{P_{14}}\\) — The split among the ancient versions shows עַלְמָה does not denote virginity
- (5) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-8}{P_{8}}\\) — Matthew's fulfilment claim requires that עַלְמָה itself denote virginity
- (6) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-10}{P_{10}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-11}{P_{11}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-14}{P_{14}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\) — *at issue, the denial of:* עַלְמָה in Isaiah 7:14 denotes a virgin, not merely a young woman

</div>

<a id="wegnerLine"></a>
**`wegnerLine`** — Wegner's grammatical objection (Isaiah 7:14)

**The Wegner line.** The predicate-adjective parse, the near-term setting
of the sign, the ordinary pregnancy that setting supplies, and the principle
that the Isaianic referent settles the word's denotation — delivering that the
עַלְמָה of the sign is pregnant when it is given.

The line stops at the pregnancy and the two further moves are closing steps,
because that is where the argument actually divides: the parse is common
ground, and everything contestable happens after it.

`lexicalSenseRequiredForFulfilment` is not among its grounds and is not
Wegner's view. He holds a prophetic pattern, on which Matthew's use of the
verse survives the lexical finding, so the objection stops at the lexical
conclusion rather than running on to the fulfilment claim.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-33}{P_{33}}\\) — הָרָה at Isaiah 7:14 is a predicate adjective: the עַלְמָה is pregnant
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-81}{P_{81}}\\) — Isaiah 7:14 is a near-term sign to Ahaz, fulfilled in Isaiah's generation
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}\\) — The pregnancy Isaiah 7:14 announces is an ordinary conception
- (4) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\) — What the עַלְמָה of Isaiah 7:14 turns out to be settles what the word denotes
- (5) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-33}{P_{33}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-34}{P_{34}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-34}{P_{34}}\\) — *at issue:* The עַלְמָה of Isaiah 7:14 is already pregnant when the sign is given

</div>

<a id="wegnerClosingSteps"></a>
**`wegnerClosingSteps`**

The two steps that carry Wegner's line to its lexical conclusion: the
pregnancy excludes virginity, and the referent settles the word. Passed to
`caseOf` as closing steps, so that a variant can change the grounds without
retyping them.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-34}{P_{34}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-36}{P_{36}}\\) — *would give:* The עַלְמָה of Isaiah 7:14 is not a virgin
- (2) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-36}{P_{36}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-37}{P_{37}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\) — *would deny:* עַלְמָה in Isaiah 7:14 denotes a virgin, not merely a young woman

</div>

<a id="signLine"></a>
**`signLine`** — The fathers' sign argument (Isaiah 7:11, 14)

**The fathers' sign argument.** Justin, Irenaeus and Origen, and every other
father the library has read on the verse, and Rydelnik today: the sign of 7:14
must be extraordinary, an ordinary conception is not, so the pregnancy is no
ordinary one. It denies the ground of Wegner's line that the parse does not
supply, and nothing else.

Its step is rated `plausible`: no source cited here grants both grounds and
holds the pregnancy ordinary. The rival denies the first ground instead, and the
grounds are rated separately. It is not rated higher, because the step reads the
conception as the whole of the sign.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-39}{P_{39}}\\) — The sign of Isaiah 7:14 must be extraordinary, like the sign offered at 7:11
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-40}{P_{40}}\\) — An ordinary conception is nothing extraordinary: it happens to all women
- (3) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-39}{P_{39}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-40}{P_{40}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}\\) — *at issue, the denial of:* The pregnancy Isaiah 7:14 announces is an ordinary conception

</div>

<a id="ordinarySignLine"></a>
**`ordinarySignLine`** — The near-term reply: a sign need not be a miracle

**The near-term reply**, as an argument: signs in Isaiah are ordinary
events, and this one is dated by a child's infancy, so it need not be
extraordinary. Wegner (469–470) and Rhodea (64–65).

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}}\\) — Signs elsewhere in Isaiah are ordinary events: his children, 8:18
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}\\) — Isaiah 7:16 dates the deliverance by a child's infancy
- (3) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-39}{P_{39}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-39}{P_{39}}\\) — *at issue, the denial of:* The sign of Isaiah 7:14 must be extraordinary, like the sign offered at 7:11

</div>

<a id="septuagintLine"></a>
**`septuagintLine`** — The Septuagint as a witness (Isaiah 7:14 in Greek)

**The Septuagint as a witness.** Irenaeus's argument: the Greek was made by
Jews long before Christ, so its "virgin" cannot be a Christian reading put on
the text. Its hinge is `parthenosMeansVirgin`, and the dispute over the
Septuagint is about that one ground.

The step draws out its grounds: a translator who chose for the woman a word that
means a virgin described her as one. It is rated `plausible`: no reader cited
here grants that the word means a virgin and denies that the translator called
her one. Bratcher and Brown, who deny the next step, grant this one: the
translator meant "a young woman, at that time virgin" (Bratcher 115), "a
deliberate preference for understanding the young woman of Isa 7:14 as a virgin"
(Brown 148).

Walton doubts the word itself, and that dissent is counted where it belongs, in
the rating of the third ground. Against the step he offers one thing more,
Archer's suggestion that the translator of Isaiah "consistently showed a tendency
to be imprecise in his choice of Greek terms", which "could well be the
explanation of the use of parthenos here" (293). That is a guess at why the
translator wrote the word, not a reading of what he wrote, and it is not counted
as a dissent. The translator's own text tells against it: everywhere else in his
Isaiah, παρθένος stands for בְּתוּלָה (23:4, 37:22, 47:1, 62:5;
`isaiahUsesParthenosForBetulah`). The step is not rated higher, because none of
its readers argues for it beyond the word's sense.

The main contest is over the third ground, rated `disputed`; the witness is no
stronger than that ground, so the step's rating changes no verdict.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — The Septuagint renders עַלְמָה at Isaiah 7:14 as παρθένος
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-15}{P_{15}}\\) — The Greek Isaiah was translated by Jews before the coming of Christ
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-16}{P_{16}}\\) — In the Greek of the Septuagint, παρθένος means a virgin
- (4) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-15}{P_{15}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-16}{P_{16}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-31}{P_{31}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-31}{P_{31}}\\) — *at issue:* Before Christ, a Jewish translator read the woman of Isaiah 7:14 as a virgin

</div>

<a id="driftLine"></a>
**`driftLine`** — Wegner on παρθένος: the word had not yet come to mean 'virgin'

**Wegner on παρθένος**: in the Septuagint's day the word meant "young
woman", and came to mean "virgin" only by the time of the New Testament
(482–83). Held by Wegner, Rhodea and Meade; disputed by Rico and Gentry, and by
Bratcher. Rhodea follows Wegner, with an "apparently", and draws from Genesis
34:3 that the word "need not refer to a virgo intacta" (67). Meade holds the
same, "cf. Dina in Gen 34:3", and that by Justin's day the word had been
"hijacked or used to mean 'chaste woman' only" (comment of 9 January 2013).

Three grounds: the older usage; what the Greek of 34:3 reads; and that the noun
there describes Dinah as she then was. The third is Wegner's own — Dinah "is
called a παρθένος even after she was raped by Shechem" (483) — and Miller's, and
it is not the text's: the order of the verses puts Shechem's love after his act,
not the noun's description (`parthenosDescribesDinahAsSheThenWas`). It is
written out, not left inside the step, so that a reader sees it.

The step is rated `disputed`, because two readers grant all its grounds and
deny its conclusion. Rico and Gentry grant the older usage, that the Greek
calls Dinah a παρθένος, and that she was then no longer a virgin; but Genesis
34:1–3 is "the exception that proves the rule" (21), an archaism of the Greek
Pentateuch, whose language is "more elevated and classical than the language of
the later texts" (18). Bratcher
grants all three — "at first the word was used in a general sense of 'girl',
'young woman'" (112), and Dinah "was no longer, therefore, a 'virgin'" — and still
finds that "parthenos definitely means 'virgin' in the LXX; only very
exceptionally (and, inexplicably, in Gen. 34:3) is it used otherwise" (113). The
Greek Isaiah, a later book by another translator, uses the word elsewhere only
for בְּתוּלָה (`isaiahUsesParthenosForBetulah`).

Delling, in the standard theological dictionary, reads the Septuagint's usage at
Isaiah 7:14 as demanding "no more than the sense of a 'woman untouched by a man
up to the moment of the conception'" (*TDNT* 5.833, as Rhodea quotes him, 67
n. 42): a virgin until then, whatever followed. And the Greek Pentateuch, the
corpus Genesis 34:3 comes from, uses the word in its laws where virginity is the
point (`lawsLine`). One passage in the broader sense does not show that the
narrower sense was missing.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-18}{P_{18}}\\) — In early Greek, παρθένος meant a young woman, with or without virginity
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-19}{P_{19}}\\) — The Septuagint calls Dinah a παρθένος at 34:3, after Shechem lies with her (34:2)
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-76}{P_{76}}\\) — At 34:3 παρθένος describes Dinah as she then was, no longer a virgin (Miller)
- (4) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-18}{P_{18}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-19}{P_{19}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-76}{P_{76}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-17}{P_{17}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-17}{P_{17}}\\) — *at issue:* In the Septuagint's day, παρθένος meant 'young woman'; not yet 'virgin'

</div>

<a id="usageLine"></a>
**`usageLine`** — Rico and Gentry: παρθένος means 'virgin' in the Greek of the Scriptures

**The case from usage.** Held by Rico and Gentry; disputed by Davidson and
Meade. Rico and Gentry argue from the Jewish objection itself: "Otherwise the
discussion of Justin and Trypho and the change from parthenos to neanis by
AQUILA, SYMMACHUS, and THEODOTION in Is 7:14 would have no raison d'être" (21).

The first ground, the Greek Isaiah's other uses of the word, is the library's
own addition, read from the two texts: it is the usage of the translator whose
word is in question, as Genesis 34:3 is not. What the texts read is not in
dispute; what it shows can be. It shows the sense "virgin" only if בְּתוּלָה
means a virgin where he renders it, and two of the four are figures for a city,
the "virgin daughter" of Zion (37:22) and of Babylon (47:1). Bratcher, who
argues from the same correspondence across the whole Septuagint — 45 of the 52
times בְּתוּלָה occurs — warns that where it means only a young girl, or is used
figuratively, "in such cases parthenos in the LXX will have the same meaning"
(113).

The step is rated `disputed`, on two readers who grant the Jewish objection and
read it the other way: the revisers were answering a sense Christians had put on
the word, not the sense its translator gave it. A. B. Davidson: the Three wrote
νεᾶνις "possibly to evade the technical sense put on the word by the
Christians", παρθένος having been "used generally for 'girl' or 'young woman'"
(*A Dictionary of the Bible* II, 1899, 456). John Meade, a Septuagint scholar
whose doctoral supervisor was Gentry, so that the dissent comes from within
Gentry's own school, finds the revisers' change sensible "only in a
context where παρθενος has been hijacked or used to mean 'chaste woman' only
(which by the time of Justin Martyr, it clearly had been, since Trypho never
disputes this point but only relies on his different version which had
νεανις)"; for "παρθενος simply means young woman in this verse and in other
places in the LXX" (comment of 9 January 2013).

The dissents on both rival steps are brief. Davidson hedges his account of the
Three with a "possibly", though not his account of the word; Meade's is a blog
comment, revising his own earlier view toward "young woman". Against Wegner's
step, Rico and Gentry give a reason, the archaism of the Greek Pentateuch, and
Bratcher calls Genesis 34:3 inexplicable without explaining it. The ratings weigh
none of this: each step has a cited reader who grants its grounds and denies its
conclusion, and so each is `disputed`. Wegner's reading can be held with all
three grounds here too — it is the countermodel in
`usage_rests_on_its_inference` — though he does not discuss the Three or Trypho.
The rating matters: rated higher, this step would decide the dispute over the
Septuagint in the witness's favour (`Dispute.Septuagint` says why).

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-20}{P_{20}}\\) — Elsewhere in the Greek Isaiah, παρθένος renders בְּתוּלָה
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-11}{P_{11}}\\) — Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion render Isaiah 7:14 with νεᾶνις
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-30}{P_{30}}\\) — Trypho rejects the Septuagint's 'the virgin' and reads 'the young woman'
- (4) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-20}{P_{20}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-11}{P_{11}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-30}{P_{30}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-16}{P_{16}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-16}{P_{16}}\\) — *at issue:* In the Greek of the Septuagint, παρθένος means a virgin

</div>

<a id="matthewReadsTheGreek"></a>
**`matthewReadsTheGreek`**

**Scripture's reading of the Greek word.** Matthew quotes the Septuagint's ἡ
παρθένος of a woman who conceived before she and Joseph came together; so in the
text he quotes, the word has the sense "virgin".

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-27}{P_{27}}\\) Matthew 1:23 quotes Isaiah 7:14 in the Greek's own words: ἡ παρθένος — *consensus*: Matt 1:23; Isa 7:14
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-28}{P_{28}}\\) Matthew says Mary conceived before she and Joseph came together — *consensus*: Matt 1:18; Matt 1:25
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-29}{P_{29}}\\) In the Greek of Isaiah 7:14, which Matthew quotes, παρθένος means 'virgin'

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\((\href{claims.html#claim-27}{P_{27}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-28}{P_{28}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-29}{P_{29}}\\).

<a id="matthewReadingSource"></a>
**`matthewReadingSource`**

The citation for Scripture's reading of the Greek word, at a confidence:
Westminster's rule that Scripture interprets Scripture (I.ix), Irenaeus on the
apostles' agreement with the Seventy (III.21.3), and Wegner, who grants Matthew's
use and denies the step (483).

```lean
def matthewReadingSource : Confidence → Source :=
  fun c =>
    {
      primary :=
        Reference.work westminsterConfession (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "I.ix"),
      supporting :=
        [Reference.work irenaeusAgainstHeresies
            (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "III.21.3"),
          Reference.work wegnerVirginBirths (Bib.Locus.page 483)],
      tradition := Tradition.reformedProtestant, confidence := c }
```

<a id="matthewLine"></a>
**`matthewLine`** — Scripture interprets Scripture: Matthew quotes ἡ παρθένος of Mary

**Scripture interprets Scripture: Matthew's quotation.** The Gospel quotes
the Greek of Isaiah 7:14, ἡ παρθένος, of Mary, who conceived "before they came
together" (1:18) and whom Joseph "knew not until she had borne a son" (1:25). If
Scripture is its own interpreter — "The infallible rule of interpretation of
Scripture is the Scripture itself" (Westminster I.ix) — the word in the text
Matthew quotes has the sense he gives it. Its grounds are Scripture alone.

Like the case from the laws, it concludes that a passage of the Septuagint uses
the word in the sense "virgin", and so, by what a usage is, that the sense was
the Septuagint's, which Wegner denies. It says nothing of the Hebrew עַלְמָה.

Cited, the step is `disputed`. Wegner grants both grounds — the word was "a
suitable term to describe Mary in the first century AD" — and denies the
conclusion: it "changed in meaning from 'young woman' to 'virgin'" between the
translator and Matthew (483). Whether that dissent counts is the question the
standards answer differently: under the evidence and tradition standards it is a
critique; under the scriptural standard, a dissent from a step whose grounds are
all Scripture counts only if it rests on Scripture alone, and Wegner's rests on
early Greek usage. `Dispute.Matthew` computes the hearing under each.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-27}{P_{27}}\\) — Matthew 1:23 quotes Isaiah 7:14 in the Greek's own words: ἡ παρθένος
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-28}{P_{28}}\\) — Matthew says Mary conceived before she and Joseph came together
- (3) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-27}{P_{27}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-28}{P_{28}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-29}{P_{29}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-29}{P_{29}}\\) — *at issue:* In the Greek of Isaiah 7:14, which Matthew quotes, παρθένος means 'virgin'

</div>

<a id="herSeedLine"></a>
**`herSeedLine`** — Luther on 'her seed': the wording itself signifies no human father

**Luther on "her seed"**: the wording itself signifies a birth with no human
father. Held by Luther and Henry, and, as "a hint", by Akin and Miravalle;
disputed by Leupold, Keil and Lewis. Irenaeus reads the verse of the Virgin's
son, though he does not argue from the wording.

Luther: the seed of other women "might rather be said to have been the seed of
the man. But that which was born from Mary was conceived of the Holy Ghost and
was the true Seed of Mary" (*Luther on the Creation* 298–99). He finds the sense
in the words of Genesis, and holds that Isaiah later "threw some additional
light" on it: "For it was then made certain that this Seed would not be born
from the union of a man and a woman" (298).

The step is rated `disputed`, because readers who grant all three grounds deny
the conclusion. Leupold reads the verse as the promise of the victor — "Both the
ultimate victory and its achievement by the seed of the woman are taught with
unequivocal plainness by this word" (167). Asked whether the expression is "so
phrased in reference to Mary and the virgin birth", he answers "Not primarily,
but at least incidentally", and holds that "the expression used does not
specifically prophesy the virgin birth" (169). Keil grants that the promise
"culminates in Christ", and finds the virgin birth in its fulfilment, "even if
the words had reference first of all to the fact that the woman had been led
astray by the serpent", "even in its apparently casual form" (102). Lewis grants
that "it is normal in Hebrew to describe descendants by the noun zeraʿ" (299);
he doubts the promise reading itself, suggesting it came from "Making the woman
to be the addressee", but argues on grounds that do not need that doubt: "To say
that the passage is messianic does not necessarily imply that it is
virgin-birth messianic" (319).

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}}\\) — Genesis 3:15 says that 'her seed' will strike the serpent's head
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}}\\) — Genesis 3:15 is the protoevangelium, the first promise of a redeemer
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-52}{P_{52}}\\) — Hebrew זֶרַע is ordinarily reckoned through the father
- (4) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-52}{P_{52}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-54}{P_{54}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-54}{P_{54}}\\) — *at issue:* The wording 'her seed' itself signifies a birth with no human father

</div>

<a id="posterityLine"></a>
**`posterityLine`** — Leupold on 'her seed': her posterity, named for the deception

**Leupold on "her seed"**: the wording names the woman's posterity, and names
the woman because she was deceived; it does not itself signify a birth with no
human father. Held by Leupold and Keil, whose two grounds Calvin gives too;
disputed by Irenaeus and Henry.

Leupold: "the expression used does not specifically prophesy the virgin birth,
but it coincides and agrees with it under divine providence. For it is not to be
forgotten that the expression 'her seed' in its first meaning is a collective
noun and includes all who are enrolled in the struggle against Satan, without
being themselves virgin born" (169).

The step is rated `disputed`. Irenaeus grants both grounds. The enmity is kept
up between the serpent and the woman's seed "until the seed did come appointed
to tread down his head" (*Against Heresies* III.23.7), and "it was by means of a
woman that he got the advantage over man at first" (V.21.1); yet he reads the
verse as preaching "He who should be born of a woman, [namely] from the Virgin"
(V.21.1), though without arguing from its wording.
Henry gives the woman's name the same reason — "because she it was whom the
devil had beguiled" — and still reads the seed as "of a woman only, of a
virgin".

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}}\\) — Genesis 3:15 says that 'her seed' will strike the serpent's head
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-56}{P_{56}}\\) — 'Her seed' at Genesis 3:15 is first collective: her posterity, not one person
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-57}{P_{57}}\\) — The seed is called the woman's because the serpent deceived the woman
- (4) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-56}{P_{56}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-57}{P_{57}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-54}{P_{54}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-54}{P_{54}}\\) — *at issue, the denial of:* The wording 'her seed' itself signifies a birth with no human father

</div>

<a id="idiomLine"></a>
**`idiomLine`** — Lewis on 'her seed': Genesis says it of Hagar and Rebekah too

**Lewis on "her seed"**: Genesis speaks of a woman's seed in ordinary births
too, so the wording at 3:15 does not by itself signify a birth with no human
father. Held by Lewis; disputed by Akin.

Lewis: "Had it been observed across history that Hagar's descendants whose
ancestral father is Abraham are also projected with a feminine possessive suffix
attached to zeraʿ (Gen 16:10), as also are Rebekah's descendants whose ancestral
father is Isaac (24:60), the treatment of Gen 3:15 would likely have been
different" (299–300). "A look at texts about Hagar and Rebekah in Genesis could
have safeguarded interpreters from the whole misguided exegetical effort" (319).

The step is rated `disputed`, on one reader. Jimmy Akin, a Catholic
apologist, does not discuss Hagar or Rebekah, but grants the point Lewis draws
from them, that a woman's seed "is not outside the bounds of Hebrew expression",
and still calls the wording "odd", and agrees with the "many" who have "rightly
seen" it as "a hint of the Virgin Birth". A hint is less than a sign, and whether
it denies Lewis's conclusion is arguable; it is the only dissent found.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}}\\) — Genesis 3:15 says that 'her seed' will strike the serpent's head
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-58}{P_{58}}\\) — Genesis speaks of a woman's seed in ordinary births: Hagar's and Rebekah's
- (3) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-58}{P_{58}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-54}{P_{54}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-54}{P_{54}}\\) — *at issue, the denial of:* The wording 'her seed' itself signifies a birth with no human father

</div>

<a id="greekHeLine"></a>
**`greekHeLine`** — The Greek's 'he': the woman's seed read as one person

**The Greek's "he"**: the translator of Genesis read the woman's seed as one
person. Held by Collins, and by Martin as Collins quotes him; Collins calls the
reading "generally acknowledged" (141). Rated `disputed`, on Philo, the earliest
known reader of this Greek, who grants that it says "he" and reads it of the
mind, a "barbarism" correct in meaning (*Allegorical Interpretation* III.188).
Lewis leaves it open: the masculine "could be an oversight", and "it is possible
that the translator reveals a messianic understanding" (300). What it does not
reach in any case is whether that person has a human father
(`Results.Genesis`).

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-59}{P_{59}}\\) — The Greek of Genesis 3:15 calls the woman's seed 'he', though σπέρμα is neuter
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-59}{P_{59}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-60}{P_{60}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-60}{P_{60}}\\) — *at issue:* The Greek translator of Genesis read the woman's seed at 3:15 as one person

</div>

##### The fulfilment of Genesis 3:15, and the critical reading

The strands above ask what the wording of Genesis 3:15 says. The reader's next
question runs the other way: the Gospel tells of one who was born of a woman,
was struck, and destroyed the devil. Does that fulfil the promise, and does the
fulfilment confirm that it was a promise?

<a id="termsMetInJesus"></a>
**`termsMetInJesus`**

**The fulfilment.** Each term of Genesis 3:15 met, as the New Testament names
it: the woman's seed in the Son "made of a woman"; the serpent in "that old
serpent, called the Devil"; its head crushed when the Son destroys the devil
"through death"; his heel struck in his death, and the wound not the end of him
in his rising. So in Jesus the promise is fulfilled.

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}}\\) Genesis 3:15 says that 'her seed' will strike the serpent's head — *consensus*: Gen 3:15; [Elliger and Rudolph 1997](../../bibliography.md#bhs-1997), app. Gen 3:15
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-64}{P_{64}}\\) Paul says God sent his Son 'made of a woman' (Galatians 4:4) — *consensus*: Gal 4:4
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-61}{P_{61}}\\) Revelation calls the devil 'that old serpent' (12:9, 20:2) — *consensus*: Rev 12:9; Rev 20:2
- (4) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-62}{P_{62}}\\) The Son came to destroy the devil and his works, through death — *consensus*: Heb 2:14; 1 John 3:8
- (5) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-63}{P_{63}}\\) Paul says Christ died, was buried, and rose the third day — *consensus*: 1 Cor 15:3-4
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-65}{P_{65}}\\) In Jesus the promise of Genesis 3:15 is fulfilled: he crushes the serpent's head

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\((\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-64}{P_{64}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-61}{P_{61}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-62}{P_{62}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-63}{P_{63}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-65}{P_{65}}\\).

<a id="fulfilmentConfirmsThePromise"></a>
**`fulfilmentConfirmsThePromise`**

**The fulfilment confirms the promise.** If in Jesus each term of Genesis
3:15 is met, the verse is a promise of him: the protoevangelium.

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-65}{P_{65}}\\) In Jesus the promise of Genesis 3:15 is fulfilled: he crushes the serpent's head — *disputed*: [Irenaeus](../../bibliography.md#irenaeus-against-heresies-180), §III.23.7; [Hamilton 2006](../../bibliography.md#hamilton-skull-crushing-seed-2006), pp. 42, 53; [Keil and Delitzsch 1866](../../bibliography.md#keil-delitzsch-pentateuch-1866), p. 102; [Westermann 1984](../../bibliography.md#westermann-genesis-1-11-1984), pp. 259–261

<a id="fulfilledInOneVirginBorn"></a>
**`fulfilledInOneVirginBorn`**

**Of the woman alone.** If the promise is fulfilled in Jesus, and Jesus was
conceived of a virgin, the seed in whom it is fulfilled had no human father.

If each of these holds,
