- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-65}{P_{65}}\\) In Jesus the promise of Genesis 3:15 is fulfilled: he crushes the serpent's head — *disputed*: [Irenaeus](../../bibliography.md#irenaeus-against-heresies-180), §III.23.7; [Hamilton 2006](../../bibliography.md#hamilton-skull-crushing-seed-2006), pp. 42, 53; [Keil and Delitzsch 1866](../../bibliography.md#keil-delitzsch-pentateuch-1866), p. 102; [Westermann 1984](../../bibliography.md#westermann-genesis-1-11-1984), pp. 259–261
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-79}{P_{79}}\\) Mary conceived Jesus while a virgin — *disputed*: Matt 1:18-25; Luke 1:26-38; [Brown 1972](../../bibliography.md#brown-problem-virginal-conception-1972), pp. 30–33

<a id="sceneMakesItAPromise"></a>

<a id="singularSyntaxNamesOne"></a>

<a id="fulfilmentSource"></a>
**`fulfilmentSource`**

The citation for the fulfilment's step, at a confidence: the readers who
argue it, and Westermann, who denies it.

```lean
def fulfilmentSource : Confidence → Source
```

<a id="fulfilmentLine"></a>
**`fulfilmentLine`** — The fulfilment of Genesis 3:15: struck at the heel, he crushes the serpent's head

**The fulfilment of Genesis 3:15**, read from Scripture: every term of the
promise is met in Jesus, as the New Testament itself names it.

- **The woman's seed**: God sent his Son, "made of a woman" (Galatians 4:4).
- **The serpent**: "that old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan" (Revelation
  12:9; 20:2).
- **Its head crushed**: the Son shared flesh and blood "that through death he
  might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil" (Hebrews
  2:14); he "was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil" (1
  John 3:8).
- **His heel struck**: he died, and rose the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4),
  a wound and not the end of him.

Irenaeus reads it so: the seed "appointed to tread down his head — which was born
of Mary", against "that old serpent" (*Against Heresies* III.23.7), and the Lord
"summed up in Himself this enmity, when He was made man from a woman, and trod
upon his head" (IV.40.3). Hamilton: the one "born of woman (i.e., her seed, Gal
4:4) who 'nullified the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil'
(Heb 2:14)—one might say he crushed the serpent's head" (53 n. 89). Keil: "In
this sense Christ is the seed of the woman, who tramples Satan under His feet,
not as an individual, but as the head" (102), with Romans 16:20 and 1 John 3:8.
Leupold, of Christ's temptation and the cross: "the first crushing defeat that
the seed of the woman administered … On the cross this victory was sealed"
(170).

**What the conclusion says, and what it does not.** That in Jesus the promise is
fulfilled: struck at the heel, he crushes the serpent's head. Calvin, Keil and
Leupold each deny that "her seed" means Christ alone — Calvin finds the word
"too violently distorted" by those who take it so, "for who will concede that a
collective noun is to be understood of one man only?" — and each holds the
conclusion as worded: "we must necessarily come to one head" (Calvin 170–71).

**The texts it rests on, and how they are linked.** Revelation's "that old
serpent" names the serpent of the garden. Romans 16:20, "the God of peace shall
bruise Satan under your feet shortly", is not counted: it is an allusion, and a
disputed one, with Calvin (171), Keil (102) and Hamilton (42) for it, and Lewis
("one possible allusion", 303) and Collins (147 n. 24, "if Paul was alluding to
this text at all") doubting it. Galatians 4:4 is cited for what it says, that
the Son was made of a woman; whether Paul alludes to Genesis there is disputed
too (`sonMadeOfAWoman`).

**Its rating.** `disputed`, on Westermann. He grants what every ground reads —
none of them says the New Testament *quotes* Genesis 3:15 — and denies that the
verse promises anyone, "even as its secondary meaning" (260), adding that
"suggestions of a messianic interpretation are found in late Judaism, but not in
the New Testament" (261). His reasons are the collective "seed" and the form of
the verse (259–60): philology and form criticism, not a reading of Hebrews,
1 John or Revelation. Lewis, who holds that "The NT never speaks of Christ as
the one who tramples the serpent" (303), denies that Scripture makes the link
but not the conclusion, and is not counted.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}}\\) — Genesis 3:15 says that 'her seed' will strike the serpent's head
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-64}{P_{64}}\\) — Paul says God sent his Son 'made of a woman' (Galatians 4:4)
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-61}{P_{61}}\\) — Revelation calls the devil 'that old serpent' (12:9, 20:2)
- (4) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-62}{P_{62}}\\) — The Son came to destroy the devil and his works, through death
- (5) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-63}{P_{63}}\\) — Paul says Christ died, was buried, and rose the third day
- (6) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-64}{P_{64}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-61}{P_{61}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-62}{P_{62}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-63}{P_{63}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-65}{P_{65}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-65}{P_{65}}\\) — *at issue:* In Jesus the promise of Genesis 3:15 is fulfilled: he crushes the serpent's head

</div>

<a id="confirmationSource"></a>
**`confirmationSource`**

The citation for the step from the fulfilment to the promise, at a
confidence: the readers who grant that Genesis 3:15 is fulfilled in Christ and
call it, for that, the first promise of the gospel.

```lean
def confirmationSource : Confidence → Source :=
  fun c =>
    { primary := Reference.work leupoldGenesis (Bib.Locus.page 167),
      supporting :=
        [Reference.work keilDelitzschPentateuch (Bib.Locus.page 102),
          Reference.work calvinGenesis (Bib.Locus.pages 170 171),
          Reference.work collinsSyntacticalNote (Bib.Locus.page 146),
          Reference.work hamiltonSkullCrushingSeed (Bib.Locus.page 31),
          Reference.work irenaeusAgainstHeresies
            (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "IV.40.3")],
      tradition := Tradition.christianTypological, confidence := c }
```

<a id="confirmationLine"></a>
**`confirmationLine`** — The fulfilment confirms the promise: Genesis 3:15 is the protoevangelium

**The fulfilment confirms the promise.** If in Jesus each term of the verse
is met, the verse was a promise of him: the protoevangelium. This is not a
deduction from Genesis alone. Reasoning "if the verse promised the Messiah, he
would crush the serpent and be struck; Jesus did; so it promised him" would
affirm the consequent. It is a step of its own: a promise whose every term is
met in one person, as Scripture names them, is a promise of that person.

Rated `plausible`. No reader found grants that Jesus fulfils the verse and
denies that it is a promise: everyone found who denies the promise, Westermann
among them, denies the fulfilment too, and that dissent belongs to the fulfilment's
step and to the claim that the verse is the protoevangelium. Everyone who grants
the fulfilment calls the verse a promise: Leupold, who finds "the ultimate
victory and its achievement by the seed of the woman … taught with unequivocal
plainness" (167); Keil (102); Calvin (170–71); Collins, for whom the verse,
read from the end, is God's threat "of an individual who will engage the snake
in combat and win" (146); Hamilton, for whom "God's first act of judgment in the
Bible is accompanied by his first promise of salvation" (31). Rated no higher,
because the step adds little to what its ground already says: to fulfil a
promise there must have been one.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-65}{P_{65}}\\) — In Jesus the promise of Genesis 3:15 is fulfilled: he crushes the serpent's head
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-65}{P_{65}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}}\\) — *at issue:* Genesis 3:15 is the protoevangelium, the first promise of a redeemer

</div>

<a id="aloneLine"></a>
**`aloneLine`** — The seed of the woman alone: the promise fulfilled in one born of a virgin

**Of the woman alone.** Granted that the promise is fulfilled in Jesus, and
that Mary conceived him as a virgin, the seed in whom it is fulfilled had no
human father. Irenaeus joins the two: "He who should be born of a woman,
[namely] from the Virgin … was preached as keeping watch for the head of the
serpent" (V.21.1).

The step only joins its grounds, and anyone who grants both grants it, so it is
rated `consensus`. What it rests on is its grounds, and both are contested: the
fulfilment on Westermann, the virginal conception on the historian this
argument cites. It reads the fact of the birth back into the promise; it does
not find the birth in the wording, which is Luther's claim and is weighed
apart (`Results.Genesis`).

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-65}{P_{65}}\\) — In Jesus the promise of Genesis 3:15 is fulfilled: he crushes the serpent's head
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-79}{P_{79}}\\) — Mary conceived Jesus while a virgin
- (3) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-65}{P_{65}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-79}{P_{79}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-66}{P_{66}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-66}{P_{66}}\\) — *at issue:* The seed in whom Genesis 3:15 is fulfilled was of the woman alone

</div>

<a id="westermannLine"></a>
**`westermannLine`** — Westermann: a punishment oracle on a line of descendants, and no promise

**Westermann's denial**: Genesis 3:15 is no promise. "The parallelism makes
it clear that 'seed' refers to a line of descendants and not to an individual"
(259), and the verse is a punishment oracle on the serpent: "It is not possible
that such a form has either promise or prophecy as its primary or even as its
secondary meaning" (260). Encoded first, as the rival to the fulfilment.

Its grounds are philology and form criticism, and so is its step: none is a
reading of another text of Scripture. Its first ground is contested in its own
right (`seedIsLineNotIndividual`, and `syntaxLine` against it).

Rated `disputed`. Calvin grants both grounds — the seed is "the posterity of the
woman generally", for "who will concede that a collective noun is to be
understood of one man only?" (170), and the verse is the serpent's sentence —
and denies the conclusion: the promise is in the curse, and "we must necessarily
come to one head" (171). Keil, who reads the seed as "the human race" and Christ
"not as an individual, but as the head" (101–2), denies it too.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-68}{P_{68}}\\) — At Genesis 3:15 'her seed' is a line of descendants, and not an individual
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-67}{P_{67}}\\) — Genesis 3:14–15 is a curse on the serpent, in the form of a punishment oracle
- (3) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-68}{P_{68}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-67}{P_{67}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}}\\) — *at issue, the denial of:* Genesis 3:15 is the protoevangelium, the first promise of a redeemer

</div>

<a id="sceneLine"></a>
**`sceneLine`** — The scene read whole: God's sentence on the serpent's power

**The scene read whole**, from the section and not the word alone: what
Genesis 3 says of the serpent, of whom the blow falls on, and of who sets the
enmity.

- **The serpent speaks, and knows the command.** It gives back God's word of
  2:17 twisted, "Ye shall not surely die" (3:4). Collins: "the snake's wording of
  v. 4 reflects knowledge of 2:17", and "animals do not have faculty of speech in
  Bible, hence there is some intervention here" (146 n. 21).
- **It is the instrument of an evil power.** Delitzsch, as Collins quotes him:
  "an animal not speaking of its own accord, but as made the instrument of itself
  by the evil principle". Woudstra: "There is a diabolical subtlety in the
  serpent's suggestions which points to a sinister background to his words"
  (197). This ground is `disputed` (`serpentIsTheInstrumentOfAPower`).
- **The blow falls on the serpent itself**: "it is the head of the serpent, not
  that of his zeraʿ, which is in view here" (Woudstra 199).
- **God sets the enmity**: "a tremendous initiative for good, unexpected and
  unmerited" (Woudstra 203).

So the sentence on the serpent is a promise of victory over the power behind it.
Collins: "the referent of the second person pronoun would actually be the dark
power behind the snake" (146–47 n. 21), and "the 'promise' for the humans is an
implicature of the punishment on the snake" (147 n. 22). Keil: "This foe is
Satan, who incessantly opposes the seed of the woman and bruises its heel, but
is eventually to be trodden under its feet" (101–2).

**Its rating.** `plausible`. Woudstra grants every ground and does not deny the
conclusion: though "this passage does not explicitly predict ultimate victory of
the woman's seed", "the One who set the enmity might also be regarded as
implicitly guaranteeing the ultimate success of those who are on his side", and
"the term 'protevangelium' may be rightly used to describe it" (203). Westermann,
who denies the conclusion, denies that the serpent is more than an animal (261),
and that dissent belongs to the ground. Von Rad, as Woudstra quotes him, denies
a protevangelium from "the sense of the passage" and the collective "seed"
(194); he is not shown to grant the grounds. Rated no higher, because the step
reads a promise out of a curse, which Collins calls "an implicature" and
Woudstra "implicit".

None of this is the reading of the readers before Christ: Jubilees, Philo and
Josephus read the serpent as an animal or an emblem, and none of them reads the
verse as a promise. It is an exegesis of the section, from its own words.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-71}{P_{71}}\\) — In Genesis 3 the serpent speaks, and knows and twists God's command
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-73}{P_{73}}\\) — The serpent of Genesis 3 is the instrument of an evil power
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-70}{P_{70}}\\) — At Genesis 3:15b the striker is singular 'he', against the serpent's own head
- (4) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-72}{P_{72}}\\) — God sets the enmity himself: 'I will put enmity' (3:15)
- (5) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-71}{P_{71}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-73}{P_{73}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-70}{P_{70}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-72}{P_{72}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}}\\) — *at issue:* Genesis 3:15 is the protoevangelium, the first promise of a redeemer

</div>

<a id="syntaxLine"></a>
**`syntaxLine`** — The syntax of the striker: 'he' who strikes is one descendant

**The syntax of the striker**, against Westermann's "a line of descendants
and not an individual". Collins: when זֶרַע "denotes a specific descendant, it
appears with singular verb inflections, adjectives, and pronouns" (144), and "the
singular pronoun hûʾ in Genesis 3:15 is quite consistent with the pattern where a
single individual is in view"; "we might wonder if the singular hûʾ in Genesis
3:15 is used precisely in order to make it plain that an individual is being
promised" (145). It is "he" who strikes "you", the serpent itself, not its seed
(146 n. 21). The Greek translator read one person (`lxxReadsOneDescendant`).
Alexander: the seed "must be understood as referring to a single individual and
not numerous descendants" (363); Leupold (166–68) and Hamilton (32) agree.

What it concludes is worded as they hold it: "her seed" at 3:15 is not only a
line of descendants, for the one who strikes is one of them, whether or not 15a
also names her posterity. Collins allows the collective too, the Messiah "as the
(primary) seed, and his followers as 'seed' by virtue of their relation to him"
(148 n. 24).

Paul reads the singular "seed" of the promise to Abraham as one person: "He
saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is
Christ" (Galatians 3:16). That is a precedent for reading the word of one, not
a reading of Genesis 3:15, and no reader found takes it as one; Calvin uses it so
("So Paul, from the seed of Abraham, leads us to Christ", 171). It is not counted
as a ground.

Rated `disputed`. Keil grants the first two grounds — "the posterity of a man may
consist of a whole tribe or of one son only", and the victory is "over the
serpent itself" — and denies that "by the seed of the woman we are to understand
one solitary person, one individual only" (101). Collins himself claims no more
than consistency, from "a fairly low level of integration" (145–46), and
Alexander notes that the same singular syntax is usually read collectively at
Genesis 22:17–18a and 24:60 (364).

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-69}{P_{69}}\\) — Elsewhere זֶרַע with singular verbs and pronouns denotes one descendant
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-70}{P_{70}}\\) — At Genesis 3:15b the striker is singular 'he', against the serpent's own head
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-60}{P_{60}}\\) — The Greek translator of Genesis read the woman's seed at 3:15 as one person
- (4) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-69}{P_{69}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-70}{P_{70}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-60}{P_{60}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-68}{P_{68}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-68}{P_{68}}\\) — *at issue, the denial of:* At Genesis 3:15 'her seed' is a line of descendants, and not an individual

</div>

<a id="lawsFixTheSense"></a>
**`lawsFixTheSense`**

**The laws' sense.** The high priest's παρθένος is set against the widow, the
woman put away, the defiled woman and the harlot, and the bride without τὰ
παρθένια dies for playing the harlot; so in these laws παρθένος is used in the
sense "virgin".

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-21}{P_{21}}\\) The high priest of the Greek Leviticus marries a παρθένος, not a widow or a harlot — *consensus*: Lev 21:13-14; Lev 21:13-14
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-22}{P_{22}}\\) In the Greek Deuteronomy, a bride without τὰ παρθένια dies for playing the harlot — *consensus*: Deut 22:13-21; Deut 22:13-21; [Liddell and Scott 1940](../../bibliography.md#liddell-scott-jones-lexicon-1940), p. 1339; [Muraoka 2009](../../bibliography.md#muraoka-lexicon-septuagint-2009), p. 535; [Lust et al. 2003](../../bibliography.md#lust-lexicon-septuagint-2003), s.v. παρθένια
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-23}{P_{23}}\\) In the Greek Pentateuch's laws, παρθένος is used in the sense 'virgin'

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\((\href{claims.html#claim-21}{P_{21}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-22}{P_{22}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-23}{P_{23}}\\).

<a id="lawsLine"></a>
**`lawsLine`** — The laws of the Greek Pentateuch: παρθένος in the sense 'virgin'

**The case from the laws.** Bratcher's, from the Greek of Leviticus 21 and
Deuteronomy 22 (102, 113): two laws of the Greek Pentateuch, the corpus Wegner
takes Genesis 34:3 from, in which virginity is what the law turns on. The laws
are in the translators' own Greek, and they are not uses of the word *of* a
virgin, which would show nothing of its sense; the passages it rests on are
where the sense is the point (`lawsUseParthenosAsVirgin`).

It concludes nothing about Isaiah 7:14. What it shows is that "virgin" was
already a sense of παρθένος in the Septuagint's Greek, which is what Wegner
denies. The step from the two passages to the Septuagint's usage is not a step
of the argument: it is what a usage "as a whole" means
(`Testimony.Ontology.Usage`), and the meanings join the laws' sense to Rico and
Gentry's claim and against Wegner's (`Meanings.BornOfAVirgin.joins`).

The step is rated `disputed`, on one reader. Robert J. Miller grants what the
laws require: virginity matters "in the law that priests can marry only women
who are virgins (Lev 21:13-14)", and the bride of Deuteronomy 22:13–21 is
charged "with not being a virgin at the time of their marriage". But "that has
to be inferred from the context": "Neither word means virgin", and "As in other
Greek literature, parthenos in the Septuagint did not by itself connote what we
mean by virginity", for where virginity matters the Greek adds "a parthenos who
has not known a man" (Genesis 24:16) (*Born Divine*).

Miller is kept, as every cited reader is, and the page shows where his reading
breaks. He says four things of the Greek. One is answered by a reading he does
not take up, one is not answered here, and two do not hold of it.

- **Genesis 34:3**: "this term refers to a rape victim after she has been
  attacked". The Greek calls Dinah a παρθένος in the verse after Shechem lies
  with her; that the noun describes her as she then was is Miller's premise,
  not the text's. Rico and Gentry explain the verse as an archaism of the Greek
  Pentateuch; the status reading reads it under the law of the seduced
  παρθένος, as the name of the standing Shechem took (`dinahLine`).
- **Genesis 24:16**: where virginity matters, the Greek adds "a parthenos who
  has not known a man". The clause is the Hebrew's own, וְאִישׁ לֹא יְדָעָהּ, and the
  Greek renders it. What it shows about either word, the page does not settle.
- **A young widow**: "Lament like a parthenos dressed in sackcloth for the
  husband of her youth (Joel 1:8)". The Greek of Joel 1:8 calls the woman
  νύμφην, a bride; its παρθεν- word, τὸν παρθενικόν, is of the husband (read
  from Rahlfs's text).
- **The translators "consistently used it to translate the Hebrew almah"**. They
  used it for עַלְמָה twice, at Genesis 24:43 and Isaiah 7:14, and elsewhere wrote
  νεᾶνις, as Rhodea, who holds Wegner's view, notes (67 and n. 34); the word
  they used consistently for was בְּתוּלָה (Bratcher 112–13).

And he does not take up τὰ παρθένια, the abstract noun by which Walton's own
test would fix the sense. The step is cited `disputed` here, on him: it is the
step's floor, and the dispute over the Septuagint weighs it there. What its
register computes is another matter (`Dispute.Miller`). Evidence a text refutes
is struck before his dissent is checked, and the Greek of Joel 1:8 refutes his
young widow; struck of it, his dissent still denies the step through Genesis
34:3, and is a credible critique under the evidence and tradition standards.
But his case from Genesis 34:3 cannot be defended in the dispute over the
Septuagint: the status reading defeats it. So his dissent is overruled, and the
step stands at the `wellSupported` its support is cited at.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-21}{P_{21}}\\) — The high priest of the Greek Leviticus marries a παρθένος, not a widow or a harlot
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-22}{P_{22}}\\) — In the Greek Deuteronomy, a bride without τὰ παρθένια dies for playing the harlot
- (3) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-21}{P_{21}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-22}{P_{22}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-23}{P_{23}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-23}{P_{23}}\\) — *at issue:* In the Greek Pentateuch's laws, παρθένος is used in the sense 'virgin'

</div>

<a id="seductionLawNamesDinah"></a>
**`seductionLawNamesDinah`**

**The law's name for Dinah.** The law of the seduced woman calls her a
παρθένος after the man has lain with her, and sets what he owes by "the
bride-price of virgins"; Genesis 34 tells Shechem's act in the words of that law
and its neighbours. So when the Greek calls Dinah "the παρθένος" at 34:3, it
names her by the standing he took, in the sense "virgin".

If each of these holds,

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-24}{P_{24}}\\) In the Greek Exodus, the seduced παρθένος is owed 'the bride-price of virgins' — *consensus*: Exod 22:15-16; Exod 22:15-16
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-25}{P_{25}}\\) Genesis 34 tells Shechem's act in the words of the laws of the violated virgin — *consensus*: Gen 34:2; Gen 34:2; Gen 34:7; Gen 34:12; Gen 34:12; Deut 22:29; Deut 22:29; Deut 22:21; Exod 22:15-16; Exod 22:15-16
- \\(\therefore\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-26}{P_{26}}\\) At Genesis 34:3 the Greek names Dinah a παρθένος as the law names the seduced virgin

</div>

In symbols, the step is \\((\href{claims.html#claim-24}{P_{24}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-25}{P_{25}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-26}{P_{26}}\\).

<a id="dinahLine"></a>
**`dinahLine`** — The law's name for Dinah: Genesis 34:3 read under Exodus 22:15–16

**The status reading of Genesis 34:3.** Wegner's case rests on one verse:
after Shechem "lay with her and humbled her" (34:2), the Greek says he "loved the
παρθένος, and spoke to her according to the mind of the παρθένος" (34:3). He
reads the word as said of her as she then was, a woman no longer a virgin, so
that it cannot mean "virgin". This line reads it the other way: as the name of
the standing Shechem took from her. A noun that names a woman says who she is in
the story, not what she is at the moment of the clause: a noun phrase is read at
a time of its own, which the context gives, not at its verb's (Enç 1986), as
Scripture names Rahab "the harlot" long after Jericho (Hebrews 11:31, James
2:25) and Matthew "the tax collector" after his call (Matthew 10:3). The order
of 34:2 and 34:3 puts Shechem's love after his act; it does not put the noun's
description there.

The law does exactly this. In the Greek Exodus a man who "deceives a παρθένος
not betrothed and lies with her" shall endow her as his wife, or, if her father
refuses, pay "the bride-price of virgins" (22:15–16). The woman he has lain with
is still the law's παρθένος, and what he owes is a virgin's price. Genesis 34
tells Shechem's act in that law's words and its neighbours': he "humbled" her
(34:2), as the man who seizes a virgin has "humbled" her (Deuteronomy 22:29);
his deed was "folly in Israel" (34:7, in the Hebrew), as the harlotry of a bride
without the tokens of virginity is (Deuteronomy 22:21); and he offers the
bride-price (34:12) that Exodus requires. So the narrative treats Dinah as the
law's violated virgin. That is the use of the word the verse shows, and on that
reading it is no evidence that παρθένος could mean a woman who is not a virgin.

Frymer-Kensky reads the law and the story the same way, from the Hebrew. The
lover "pays the mohar habbetulot even if the father refuses to allow him to
marry her", a price a seduced girl "would no longer command" (80); and she
follows the Dinah story with the law of "Intercourse with an Unmarried Girl
(Exodus 22.15-16 and Deuteronomy 22.28-29)", under which the father "can take the
'virgin's brideprice' from the lover" (91). She hedges the price in a note: it
"might simply mean the appropriate brideprice for young girls" (80 n. 3). She
does not discuss the Greek of 34:3.

**What it does not settle.** The Hebrew of 34:3 has נַעֲרָה, "girl", and the
translator of Genesis renders that word with παρθένος elsewhere, of Rebekah
(24:14, 16, 55), and with παῖς (24:28, 57). At 34:4 and 34:12, where marriage
and the bride-price are in view, he writes παῖς for Dinah, not παρθένος. Rico
and Gentry read 34:3 as the older, broader usage, an archaism of the Greek
Pentateuch, while the Septuagint's Greek at large means "virgin" by the word
(18, 21). Bratcher finds 34:3 "surprising", since Dinah "was no longer,
therefore, a 'virgin' in the technical sense of the word" (113). The Greek
Deuteronomy does not tell either way: its translator writes νεᾶνις for נַעֲרָה
through chapter 22, of the virgin wrongly accused (22:19) as of the woman seized
(22:29), so his change of word follows the Hebrew, not the woman's state.

**Its rating.** `plausible`. A step is `disputed` when a cited reader grants its
grounds and denies its conclusion, and none has been found who does. Wegner,
Rhodea, Meade, Rico and Gentry and Bratcher read 34:3 as said of a woman who is
not a virgin, but none of them takes up Exodus 22:15–16 or the law's words in
Genesis 34, the second ground. Frymer-Kensky grants that ground, and does not
deny the conclusion; her note doubts what the first ground's law prices, and so
bears on how firmly that law is read, not on this step. No reader has been found
who makes the status reading of the Greek: it is built here from the texts, with
Frymer-Kensky's reading of the Hebrew, and is rated no higher than `plausible`
for that reason. The commentaries on the Greek Genesis that might settle it,
Wevers's *Notes* and Harl's *La Genèse*, have not been read. A reader of them who
has the law before him and still reads 34:3 of a woman no longer a virgin would
make the step `disputed`; and the verdict of `Dispute.Septuagint` turns on this
rating.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-24}{P_{24}}\\) — In the Greek Exodus, the seduced παρθένος is owed 'the bride-price of virgins'
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-25}{P_{25}}\\) — Genesis 34 tells Shechem's act in the words of the laws of the violated virgin
- (3) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-24}{P_{24}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-25}{P_{25}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-26}{P_{26}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-26}{P_{26}}\\) — *at issue:* At Genesis 34:3 the Greek names Dinah a παρθένος as the law names the seduced virgin

</div>

##### The two defeaters, as arguments in their own right

`criticalDenialUnderBerry` and `criticalDenialUnderParity` ask what the critical
line is left with once a reply is in play. The lines below ask something else:
what each reply *concludes*, taken on its own. Written this way a reply is a
position with premises of its own, and so a node that can defeat, and be
defeated by, the line it answers — see `Dispute.lean`.

##### What the strands share

<a id="sharedGrounds"></a>
**`sharedGrounds`**

The premises no single strand owns: Mary's conception, and the agreement of
the two birth narratives about it. Every scriptural package needs them and
none of the four strands delivers them.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-79}{P_{79}}\\) — Mary conceived Jesus while a virgin
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-80}{P_{80}}\\) — Matthew and Luke are independent traditions agreeing on the virgin conception

</div>

<a id="scripturalLines"></a>
**`scripturalLines`**

The four scriptural strands, in the order the module doc introduces them.
`christian` is exactly these four on shared ground.

```lean
def scripturalLines : List (Line Claim) :=
  [isaianicLine, protoevangeliumLine,
    micheanLine, compositionalLine]
```

##### How the variants are written

A handful of these packages are positions someone holds; the rest exist to be
*refuted*, because "this premise is load-bearing" is proved by removing it and
exhibiting a countermodel, and the package with it removed has to be written
down to be refuted. So the file grows with every result, and counting it here
would only be one more thing to keep current.

Each variant is a named difference from `christian`: one line on different
grounds, or one fewer line. Before `Line` existed each restated the whole
twenty-one element premise list, where a reader could not see which premise had
gone and a slip in the other twenty was invisible.

Two packages are *not* built from the lines, and deliberately. `critical`
grants the texts and denies every inference drawn from them, so its premises
group by kind rather than by strand. `lexicalCriticalUnderCompatibility` mixes
the objector's grounds with the replies to them. Forcing either into `caseOf`
would describe them as something they are not.

<a id="christian"></a>
**`christian`** — Scriptural reading of Isaiah 7:14, Genesis 3:15 and Micah 5:2–3

The scriptural argument: four strands, no appeal to magisterial
authority.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-1}{P_{1}}\\) — Isaiah 7:14 is a Messianic prediction of a virgin birth
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\) — עַלְמָה in Isaiah 7:14 denotes a virgin, not merely a young woman
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — The Septuagint renders עַלְמָה at Isaiah 7:14 as παρθένος

<a id="critical"></a>
**`critical`** — Critical reading: near-term sign, etiology, and silence

The critical reading: the quotation, the Septuagint rendering and the
wording of Genesis and Micah are all granted, and every inference drawn from
them is denied.

Written flat rather than from the lines above, because that is its shape: the
texts first, then the critical readings of them, then the denials. It is not
four strands on shared ground; it is the refusal of four strands.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — The Septuagint renders עַלְמָה at Isaiah 7:14 as παρθένος

- (4) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-77}{P_{77}}\\) — Micah 5:3 names only the woman in labour as bearing the coming ruler
- (5) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-81}{P_{81}}\\) — Isaiah 7:14 is a near-term sign to Ahaz, fulfilled in Isaiah's generation
- (6) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-82}{P_{82}}\\) — A sign given for Ahaz's generation is not also a prediction of a virgin birth
- (7) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-88}{P_{88}}\\) — Genesis 3:15 is an etiology of snake-human enmity, 'her seed' her descendants
- (8) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-89}{P_{89}}\\) — Micah's silence about a father is an argument from silence and proves nothing
- (9) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\) — *denied:* עַלְמָה in Isaiah 7:14 denotes a virgin, not merely a young woman
- (10) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}}\\) — *denied:* Genesis 3:15 is the protoevangelium, the first promise of a redeemer
- (11) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-53}{P_{53}}\\) — *denied:* The matrilineal wording of Genesis 3:15 marks a birth with no human father
- (12) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-78}{P_{78}}\\) — *denied:* Micah's mention of a mother and no father indicates a birth with no human father
- (13) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-81}{P_{81}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-82}{P_{82}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-1}{P_{1}}\\) — *would deny:* Isaiah 7:14 is a Messianic prediction of a virgin birth
- (14) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-1}{P_{1}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-44}{P_{44}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-93}{P_{93}}\\) — *would give:* The Messiah must be born of a virgin
- (15) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-52}{P_{52}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-53}{P_{53}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-93}{P_{93}}\\) — *would give:* The Messiah must be born of a virgin

- (17) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-93}{P_{93}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-79}{P_{79}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-94}{P_{94}}\\)

##### Wegner's objection, and the circle in it

Four variants of one line, each a named difference. `wegnerLine` grants
everything Wegner needs; the rest take one ground away and put in its place the
step that is supposed to supply it.

<a id="wegnerLexical"></a>
**`wegnerLexical`** — Wegner's grammatical objection: the עַלְמָה is already pregnant

**Wegner's objection at full strength**, granted every premise it needs:
the predicate-adjective parse, the near-term setting of the sign, the ordinary
pregnancy that setting supplies, and the principle that the Isaianic referent
settles the word's denotation.

Stated first and in full, because the results that follow are about where its
weight rests and are worth nothing against a weakened rival.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-33}{P_{33}}\\) — הָרָה at Isaiah 7:14 is a predicate adjective: the עַלְמָה is pregnant
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-81}{P_{81}}\\) — Isaiah 7:14 is a near-term sign to Ahaz, fulfilled in Isaiah's generation
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}\\) — The pregnancy Isaiah 7:14 announces is an ordinary conception
- (4) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\) — What the עַלְמָה of Isaiah 7:14 turns out to be settles what the word denotes
- (5) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-33}{P_{33}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-34}{P_{34}}\\) — *would give:* The עַלְמָה of Isaiah 7:14 is already pregnant when the sign is given
- (6) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-34}{P_{34}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-36}{P_{36}}\\) — *would give:* The עַלְמָה of Isaiah 7:14 is not a virgin
- (7) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-36}{P_{36}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-37}{P_{37}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\) — *at issue, the denial of:* עַלְמָה in Isaiah 7:14 denotes a virgin, not merely a young woman

</div>

No premise here rests on scripture alone.

<a id="fulfilmentCase"></a>
**`fulfilmentCase`** — The fulfilment of Genesis 3:15 confirms the promise

**The fulfilment, confirming the promise**, as a position: every term of
Genesis 3:15 met in Jesus as the New Testament names it, and so the verse a
promise of him. Two steps, each rated: the fulfilment (`fulfilmentLine`) and the
confirmation (`confirmationLine`). The confirmation's ground is the fulfilment's
conclusion, so it enters as a step, not as a premise.

- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-64}{P_{64}}\\) — Paul says God sent his Son 'made of a woman' (Galatians 4:4)
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-61}{P_{61}}\\) — Revelation calls the devil 'that old serpent' (12:9, 20:2)
- (4) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-62}{P_{62}}\\) — The Son came to destroy the devil and his works, through death
- (5) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-63}{P_{63}}\\) — Paul says Christ died, was buried, and rose the third day
- (6) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-50}{P_{50}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-64}{P_{64}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-61}{P_{61}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-62}{P_{62}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-63}{P_{63}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-65}{P_{65}}\\) — *would give:* In Jesus the promise of Genesis 3:15 is fulfilled: he crushes the serpent's head
- (7) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-65}{P_{65}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}}\\) — *at issue:* Genesis 3:15 is the protoevangelium, the first promise of a redeemer

</div>

one fulfils it. He holds the confirmation's step with the fulfilment's side —
what is fulfilled was promised — and runs it the other way: suggestions of a
messianic reading "are found in late Judaism, but not in the New Testament"
(261). So his denial that the verse is a promise is a denial that it is
fulfilled in Jesus, and the package says so.

- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-51}{P_{51}}\\) — *at issue, the denial of:* Genesis 3:15 is the protoevangelium, the first promise of a redeemer

</div>

No premise here rests on scripture alone.

<a id="septuagintToTheWordSource"></a>
**`septuagintToTheWordSource`**

How the step from the translator's reading to Isaiah's word is rated:
Irenaeus takes it, against Theodotion and Aquila (*Against Heresies* III.21.1),
because he holds the Greek "interpreted by the inspiration of God" (III.21.2).
`disputed`: Bratcher grants that the translator read a virgin (115) and denies
that עַלְמָה says so (105–106); Brown grants the translator's "deliberate
preference" (*Birth of the Messiah* 148) and denies that the Hebrew stresses
virginity (147); and Walton holds that the Greek shows at best "an
interpretational preference rather than a linguistic necessity" (293). See
`translatorsReadingFixesTheWord`.

```lean
def septuagintToTheWordSource : Source :=
  {
    primary :=
      Reference.work irenaeusAgainstHeresies (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "III.21.1"),
    supporting :=
      [Reference.work irenaeusAgainstHeresies (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "III.21.2"),
        Reference.work bratcherStudyOfIsaiah (Bib.Locus.pages 105 106),
        Reference.work bratcherStudyOfIsaiah (Bib.Locus.page 115),
        Reference.work brownBirthMessiah (Bib.Locus.pages 147 148),
        Reference.work waltonWhatsInAName (Bib.Locus.page 293)],
    tradition := Tradition.christianTypological,
    confidence := Confidence.disputed }
```

<a id="septuagintOnTheWord"></a>
**`septuagintOnTheWord`** — The Septuagint as a witness to what עַלְמָה means

**The Septuagint asked for Isaiah's word**: its witness, with the step from
the translator's reading to what עַלְמָה denotes added. That step is rated
`disputed`, and the case is only as good as it is.

- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-15}{P_{15}}\\) — The Greek Isaiah was translated by Jews before the coming of Christ
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-16}{P_{16}}\\) — In the Greek of the Septuagint, παρθένος means a virgin
- (4) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-9}{P_{9}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-15}{P_{15}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-16}{P_{16}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-31}{P_{31}}\\) — *would give:* Before Christ, a Jewish translator read the woman of Isaiah 7:14 as a virgin
- (5) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-31}{P_{31}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-2}{P_{2}}\\) — *at issue:* עַלְמָה in Isaiah 7:14 denotes a virgin, not merely a young woman

##### How the results are checked

Every result is tagged `@[headline]` and followed by `#print axioms`, so its
trust base is visible in the source. Entailments are established with
`establish`; refutations name a countermodel and use `refute_with`. A
countermodel here is the rival's reading written down as a valuation, which is
why each one is a named definition with a docstring saying what position it
encodes rather than an anonymous function.

#### Results

<a id="christian_establishes"></a>
**`christian_establishes`**

Given the scriptural premises, the conclusion follows.

```lean
theorem christian_establishes : Establishes christian
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="catholic_establishes"></a>
**`catholic_establishes`**

The Roman Catholic package establishes it too, unsurprisingly: it is the
scriptural package with a further strand bolted on.

```lean
theorem catholic_establishes : Establishes catholic
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="magisterialOnly_establishes"></a>
**`magisterialOnly_establishes`**

The magisterial route carries the conclusion on its own, for a reader who
grants the authority it claims.

```lean
theorem magisterialOnly_establishes : Establishes magisterialOnly
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="criticalReading"></a>
**`criticalReading`**

The critical reading, written down: עַלְמָה means "young woman", Isaiah's
sign was given to Ahaz, Genesis 3:15 is an etiology, and Micah's silence about a
father is only silence. No virgin-birth criterion arises.

```lean
def criticalReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.almahMeansVirgin => False
    | Claim.isaiahPredictsVirginBirth => False
    | Claim.genesis3_15IsProtoevangelium => False
    | Claim.seedOfTheWomanImpliesNoHumanFather => False
    | Claim.maternalSilenceImpliesNoHumanFather => False
    | Claim.messiahBornOfVirgin => False
    | Claim.jesusSatisfiesCriterion => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="critical_not_establishes"></a>
**`critical_not_establishes`**

The critical reading does not establish the conclusion.

```lean
theorem critical_not_establishes : ¬Establishes critical
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="criticalDenial_establishes"></a>
**`criticalDenial_establishes`**

The critical case for the denial does go through on its own terms. Stating
it as an argument rather than a bare assumption is what makes the next result
possible.

```lean
theorem criticalDenial_establishes : Establishes criticalDenial
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="berryReading"></a>
**`berryReading`**

Berry's reading, written down: the sign was given to Ahaz, how it was
fulfilled in his day is unclear, and so the near-term reading does not exclude
a further referent — leaving the predictive reading standing.

```lean
def berryReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.nearTermExcludesMessianicSense => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="berry_blocks_critical_denial"></a>
**`berry_blocks_critical_denial`**

**Berry's objection blocks the critical denial.** Grant that Isaiah 7:14
was a sign to Ahaz, and grant with Berry that how it was fulfilled in Ahaz's own
day is an open question, and the denial no longer follows.

This is the narrow thing the objection does, and it is worth being clear about
what it does not do. It does not establish the predictive reading, and it does
not touch the lexical dispute. It removes one route to the denial — the route
that runs through the near-term fulfilment — and leaves the argument where
`hinges_jointly_load_bearing` puts it.

```lean
theorem berry_blocks_critical_denial : ¬Establishes criticalDenialUnderBerry
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="parityReading"></a>
**`parityReading`**

The parity reading, written down: a near-term Assyrian setting is simply not
the kind of reason that rules out messianic reference, since Isaiah 9 and 11 sit
on that same timeline and are read messianically anyway.

```lean
def parityReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.nearTermExcludesMessianicSense => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="parity_blocks_critical_denial"></a>
**`parity_blocks_critical_denial`**

**Postell's parity argument blocks the critical denial too**, and by a
different route from Berry's.

Berry's objection is evidential — we do not know how the sign was fulfilled in
Ahaz's day. Parity is structural — the near-term setting was never the right
kind of reason, because Isaiah 9:5–6 and 11:1–10 stand on the same Assyrian
timeline and are read messianically without embarrassment. An opponent who
answers Berry by settling the near-term referent has not touched this.

```lean
theorem parity_blocks_critical_denial : ¬Establishes criticalDenialUnderParity
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="reformedReading"></a>
**`reformedReading`**

The Reformed objection, written down: papal teaching says what it says, and
saying it settles nothing, because Scripture is the supreme judge.

```lean
def reformedReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.magisteriumIsDoctrinallyAuthoritative => False
    | Claim.messiahBornOfVirgin => False
    | Claim.jesusSatisfiesCriterion => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="magisterial_authority_is_load_bearing"></a>
**`magisterial_authority_is_load_bearing`**

**What the magisterial strand is worth to a reader who does not grant the
magisterium's authority: nothing.** Deny that premise and the route collapses
outright, however firmly the teaching itself is attested.

This is why `christian` excludes it. A reader who holds with Westminster I.x
that Scripture is the supreme judge of controversies loses the whole of
`magisterialOnly` and must get the criterion from the four scriptural strands
or not at all.

```lean
theorem magisterial_authority_is_load_bearing : ¬Establishes magisterialDenied
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="almah_not_load_bearing"></a>
**`almah_not_load_bearing`**

**The lexical premise no longer carries the argument.** Strip `almah` and
the protoevangelium and Michean strands still deliver the criterion.

Before Genesis 3:15 and Micah 5:2–3 were encoded, this module proved the
opposite — and `almah_is_load_bearing_alone` below shows that the earlier
finding was right about the Isaianic strand taken by itself. What changed is
not the Isaianic evidence but the number of strands.

```lean
theorem almah_not_load_bearing : Establishes christianWithoutAlmah
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="withoutAlmahReading"></a>
**`withoutAlmahReading`**

A reading that grants everything in the Isaianic strand except the lexical
premise.

```lean
def withoutAlmahReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.almahMeansVirgin => False
    | Claim.messiahBornOfVirgin => False
    | Claim.jesusSatisfiesCriterion => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="almah_is_load_bearing_alone"></a>
**`almah_is_load_bearing_alone`**

Within the Isaianic strand taken alone, the lexical premise is still
load-bearing: remove it and that strand yields nothing. The earlier
single-stranded encoding of this module is preserved here rather than deleted,
because it is what makes `almah_not_load_bearing` informative — the Isaianic
evidence did not get stronger, it got company.

```lean
theorem almah_is_load_bearing_alone : ¬Establishes isaianicStrandWithoutAlmah
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="admissibility_is_not_enough"></a>
**`admissibility_is_not_enough`**

**Admissibility is not enough.** Berry's lexical point is defensive — the
semantic range of עַלְמָה does not *exclude* the sense "virgin" — and defensive
is all it is. Substitute it for `almahMeansVirgin` and the Isaianic strand
yields nothing, on the same reading that refutes the strand without any lexical
premise at all.

The gap between *may mean* and *does mean* is where this argument lives, and
Berry is useful against the critical denial without narrowing it.

```lean
theorem admissibility_is_not_enough : ¬Establishes
    isaianicStrandOnAdmissibility
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

##### The referential strand

<a id="semantic_establishes"></a>
**`semantic_establishes`**

**The referential argument goes through.** Granted only what both sides
grant about the word — that עַלְמָה denotes a young woman of marriageable age,
and that being a virgin does not exclude a woman from that denotation — and
granted that Mary was such a woman and conceived as a virgin, Matthew's claim
turns out not to have required the lexical sense at all.

Nothing here asserts that עַלְמָה *means* virgin. The argument is about
reference, not sense, and it is cheaper for exactly that reason.

```lean
theorem semantic_establishes : Establishes semantic
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="lexicalCritical_establishes"></a>
**`lexicalCritical_establishes`**

The lexical objection, written down and granted its own premises.

```lean
theorem lexicalCritical_establishes : Establishes lexicalCritical
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="compatibilityReading"></a>
**`compatibilityReading`**

The referential reading, written down: the versions differ about which term
to use and not about who is described, so the divergence settles nothing about
the sense, and Matthew's claim never needed the sense.

```lean
def compatibilityReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.versionalDivergenceRefutesVirginSense => False
    | Claim.lexicalSenseRequiredForFulfilment => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="compatibility_defeats_lexical_objection"></a>
**`compatibility_defeats_lexical_objection`**

**The referential reply defeats the lexical objection.** Keep every
versional datum — the Targum's עוּלֵימְתָא, the Three's νεᾶνις, the Septuagint's
παρθένος, the Peshitta's ܒܬܘܠܬܐ, Qumran's confirmation of the Hebrew — add the
referential premises, and the objection no longer reaches its conclusion.

The tension in the versions is not evidence against the reading once virginity
is compatible with the word. It is evidence that four translators made four
defensible choices about how much of the referent's description to make
explicit.

```lean
theorem compatibility_defeats_lexical_objection : ¬Establishes
    lexicalCriticalUnderCompatibility
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="compatibilityOnlyReading"></a>
**`compatibilityOnlyReading`**

A reading on which Mary fits Isaiah's description and no criterion arises
from it.

```lean
def compatibilityOnlyReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.lexicalSenseRequiredForFulfilment => False
    | Claim.messiahBornOfVirgin => False
    | Claim.jesusSatisfiesCriterion => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="compatibility_does_not_establish_criterion"></a>
**`compatibility_does_not_establish_criterion`**

**What the referential argument costs.** It is purely defensive. It defeats
the objection without establishing the criterion: ask the same premises for
`jesusSatisfiesCriterion` and they do not deliver it, because nothing in them
says the Messiah *must* be born of a virgin — only that Mary may be described
as Isaiah describes.

This is the honest price of the move, and it is worth paying. The criterion has
to come from the Isaianic, protoevangelium or Michean strands; what the
referential argument buys is that losing the lexical dispute no longer costs
the fulfilment claim. Winning `almahMeansVirgin` outright was never necessary,
and this says so in a form either side can check.

```lean
theorem compatibility_does_not_establish_criterion : ¬Establishes
    semanticReachingForCriterion
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="noHingeReading"></a>
**`noHingeReading`**

A reading on which none of the four interpretive hinges holds: *almah*
means "young woman", the matrilineal wording of Genesis 3:15 implies nothing
about a father, Micah's silence is only silence, and Isaiah's composition does
not govern the sense of 7:14. Every textual observation is granted.

```lean
def noHingeReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.almahMeansVirgin => False
    | Claim.seedOfTheWomanImpliesNoHumanFather => False
    | Claim.maternalSilenceImpliesNoHumanFather => False
    | Claim.compositionGovernsMeaning => False
    | Claim.messiahBornOfVirgin => False
    | Claim.jesusSatisfiesCriterion => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="hinges_jointly_load_bearing"></a>
**`hinges_jointly_load_bearing`**

**The result worth having.** No single hinge carries the argument, but the
four of them jointly do: remove all four and the criterion no longer follows,
with every textual and historical premise retained.

So the argument no longer hangs on the sense of עַלְמָה alone. It hangs on that
*or* on the matrilineal wording of Genesis 3:15 *or* on Micah's maternal
silence *or* on Postell's compositional reading — and an opponent must defeat
all four. That is a materially stronger position than the single-stranded
version, and a materially weaker one than four independent arguments would be:
three of the four hinges are `disputed` for good reason, and the module doc
says why.

```lean
theorem hinges_jointly_load_bearing : ¬Establishes christianWithoutAnyHinge
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="jesus_satisfies_virgin_birth"></a>
**`jesus_satisfies_virgin_birth`**

End to end: under the scriptural package, Jesus satisfies the virgin-birth
criterion.

```lean
theorem jesus_satisfies_virgin_birth : Satisfies jesus bornOfAVirgin
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

##### Satisfiability

`Entails` is vacuously true over a premise set with no model, so a package built
from contradictory premises would establish its conclusion with every gate
passing. Only packages carrying a positive `Establishes` result need checking:
one with a `¬ Establishes` result is satisfiable already, its countermodel being
a valuation on which every premise holds.

Several packages here *deny* a premise, so the all-holds reading will not serve
them — a model has to be the position's own world, which is the same discipline
the countermodels follow.

Not tagged `@[headline]`: these are claims about the health of the encoding.

<a id="everythingHoldsReading"></a>
**`everythingHoldsReading`**

The reading on which every claim holds at once.

```lean
def everythingHoldsReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun x => True
```

<a id="christian_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`christian_is_satisfiable`**

The scriptural package has a model.

```lean
theorem christian_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable christian.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

  fun a =>
    match a with

    | x => True

The lexical objection's own world: the versions read the broad term, so

    match a with
    | Claim.almahMeansVirgin => False
    | Claim.jesusSatisfiesCriterion => False
    | x => True
